SHRI JAGMOHAN: Sir, the first poin t is that the figure which he is 
referring to pertains to the Ninth Five-Year Plan. In the tenth Five-Year Plan, 
the total focus of the scheme has been changed and now we are developing 
hubs of culture, tourism and good civic life. In the Ninth Five-Year Plan the total 
number of projects sanctioned for Rajasthan were 72 out of which 53 are still 
incomplete and the total cost which has been indicated by me is Rs. 11.64 
crores. But the hon. Member wants to know whether Rajasthan has been fairly 
treated or not. In fact, out of these plans which I have with me, I have given at 
least one great hub of culture, touris m and good civic life in every State. In 
Rajasthan I have given three—Kumbhalgarh, Chittorgarh and Jaisalmer—and a 
separate triangle around Shikhavati Bikaner temple is being worked out. Now, 
there is a total investment of Rs. 18 cr ores during the last eight months and I 
have given the figures which include Dilwada with Rs. 3 crores, Chitrakoot, Rs.

that, investments have been made at Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh. And these 
projects are being directly handled by us . In the Ninth Five-Year Plan, the total

the maximum investment has been made fo r Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and 
Gujarat.

Higher interest rates in RRBs 
*382. SHRI RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that interest rates in Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) 
are higher than those of commercial banks; and 
(b) if so, the action proposed to take up the right type of restructuring plan 
for RRBs? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) A Statem ent is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) The interest rate structure of  Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) is 
generally more or less similar to that of the commercial banks/sponsor 
banks operating in their area of operation. 
As part of financial sector reforms, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
deregulated the interest rate structure in the Banking Sector. The Board of 
Directors of each RRB is free to decide t heir interest rate structure taking into 
account the cost of funds, competitive rates in their command area, yield of 
loans/investments, establishment cost, etc. 
(b) To facilitate strengthening and revitalisation of RRBs the following 
policy initiatives have been taken:— 
• recapitalisation of 187 RRBs; 
• diversification of business portfolio and activities; 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
• rationalisation of branch network including relocation and merger 
of loss-making branches; and 
• providing greater role to the sponsor banks in the management 
of RRBs. 
Further, Government had constituted a Working Group to review the 
RRB Act, 1976. The Working Group was required to review the progress in 
dispensation of rural credit especialy through RRBs since their inception and 
to make detailed recommendations in regard to legal, regulatory, supervisory, 
institutional and technological dimensions for making RRBs-an effective 
instrument for development and growth of the rural economy. The Working 
Group has submitted its report to Government, which is under consideration. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, I would like to know whether some 
of the RRBs have closed shop and shifted to towns, without redeploying the 
resources in the rural areas where they we re mobilised, as is evident from the 
low credit-deposit ratio of 41 % and the in vestment-deposit ratio of 70%. What 
type of reforms are proposed in respect of the Regional Rural Banks in order 
to benefit the weaker sections of the society? 
SHRi JASWANT SINGH: Sir, as for the figures the hon. Member has 
cited, about certain specif ic RRBs, it is altogether different. But, so far as 
reform or reforming the Regional Rural Banks is concerned, the hon. Member 
knows that the Chalapati Rao Committee, which was constituted to go into this 
question, has given its recommendations. Without taking much time of the 
House, I can share with the h on. Members some of the major 
recommendations of the Committee. Ther e is recommendation for change in 
the capital structure and ownership pattern , about the structural consolidation, 
about the size of the Board and the role  and functions of the Chairman and 
also regulatory framework and capital adequacy. It is a very comprehensive 
Report. There has been some improvement in the last decade or so in the 
functioning of the RRBs, and we will continue to monitor the progress of the 
RRBs. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir,  my second supplementary is, 
whether the merger of weak RRBs with commercial banks has proved 
beneficial. If so, the details thereof. In case of merger, how will the promotion 
problems of the staff of RRBs would be solved? 
8 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Si r, compared to the commercial banks, the 
origin of the RRBs is different. The RRBs were really started—or meant 
specifically—for lending to the farming community, artisans, etc. Then, around 
1993-94, they were brought into the pattern of large commercial banking 
sector; and now they really operate as any ordinary bank. But, so far as the total 
percentage to agriculture lending is concerned, the RRBs are contributing only 
about seven per cent to the agricultural sector, 41 or 43 per cent is being provided 
by the cooperative banks; and 52 per cent is being provided by the commercial 
banks. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, the hon. Minister has stated in the last 
part of his answer that one of the terms and conditions of the Working Group)—
this Group was setup to review the RRB Act of 1976, and its Report is how

rural credit, the RRBs were established on 2nd October, 1975. May I know from

available with the hon. Minister—What percentage of rural credit is today 
institutionalised through the RRBs and through other institutional arrangements,

what percentage of rural credit is given through the institutional mechanism. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, just now, I gave the percentage. Of course, 
the hon. Member is quite right, as he had been the country's Finance Minister, 
that lt the establishment of Regional Rural Banks was, without doubt, motivated 
by the factor of providing a specific instrument for agricultural lending, for rural 
lending. Thereafter, in 1993-94 or so, when whole nature of RRBs was 
changed, and as of now—I shared it with the hon. Members—the percentage of 
rural agricultural credit which is being provided by the RRBs is only about seven 
per cent of the total; 52 per cent is being provided by the commercial banks; 
and about 41 per cent is being provided by the cooperative banks. The 
Chalapati Rao Committee's recommendations have been received, and I have 
no difficulty in sending you a copy of the recommendations.

Permission for opening Foreign Currency (Domestic) Account 
*394. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE A ND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Governm ent with a view to further liberalise 
foreign exchange facilities have decided to permit resident Indians to open, 
hold and maintain foreign currency (domestic) account with any Nationalised 
Bank; 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
(c) whether any limit has been fixed for retaining money in the proposed 
foreign currency (domestic) account in US Dollars; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
36 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) Yes Sir. As a significant step towards further 
liberalization of foreign exchange facilities available to individual residents, the 
RBI has permitted a person resident in India, to open, hold and maintain with 
an Authorized Dealer in India a Foreign Currency Account known as Resident 
Foreign Currency (Domestic) Account. Foreign Exchange acquired from any of 
the following sources can be kept in this account by Residents: 
(i) while on visit to any place outside India by way of payment for 
services not arising from any business in-or anything done in India; 
or 
(ii) from any person not resident in Indi a and who is on a visit to India, as 
honorarium or gift or for services rendered or in settlement of any 
lawful obligation; or 
(iii) by way of honorarium or gift while on a visit to any place outside India; 
or 
(iv) represents the unspent amount of foreign exchange acquired by him 
from an authorized person for travel abroad. 
This new facility is in addition to the existing facility of retaining US$2000 
or its equivalent in the form of currency notes and/or foreign currency travellers 
cheques. The balance in Resident Foreign currency (Domestic) account may 
be used for any purpose permissible under the current foreign exchange 
regulations for resident Indians (e.g. travel, medical treatment abroad, gifts upto 
US$ 5000, purchase of books directly or through the internet, education abroad, 
etc.) 
There is no limit on balances kept in Resident Foreign Currency 
(Domestic) Account. This account will be maintained in the form of a current 
account only with cheque facility.

Financial crisis in Maharashtra 
2749. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item, 
"Crisis downgrades Maharashtra to default category", which appeared in the 
'Indian Express' dated the 17th October, 2002; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) what steps are proposed to be taken to address the various 
problems and bottlenecks ment ioned in the news article to rectify the financial 
crisis in Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The article in 
the Indian Express dated 17th October, 2002 referes to the downgraded credit 
rating of the bonds issued by the Public Sector Undertakings under 
Government of Maharashtra in view of their inability to meet in time the payment 
of interest and principal obligations, due to sagging financial condition of the 
State Government. 
(b) and (c) The financial crisis faced by some States including 
Government of Maharashtra has received the attention of Government of India. 
Though the primary responsibility for the repayment of debt of State 
Government rests with respective States and the State Governments are 
expected to take adequate measures to improve their financial conditions, 
Government of India has been facilitating the States to overcome their temporary 
cash imbalance problems by making feasible releases of the State's entitlements 
in advance. 
Besides to enable fiscal consolidation, the Government of India have 
enjoined States to draw up Medium Term Fiscal Reforms Programmes 
(MTFRP) which is projected to bring down the consolidated debt of States. The 
build-up of debt and issuance of guarantees in future has been strictly capped by 
the MTFRPs, and require specific permission of Government of India u nder 
Article 293(3) of the Constitution. 
Government of Maharashtra has drawn up their Medium Term Fiscal Reform 
Programme. Further, the Government of India has since put 
102 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
forward a proposal for debt swap to enable the States to retire high cost debt so 
as to supplement their efforts towards fiscal consolidation.

2752. SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: Wi ll the Minister of FINANCE AND

COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that the lending rates of banks have

Risk-Based Supervision for Banks 
2759. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Reserve Bank of India propose to introduce Risk Based 
Supervision (RBS) for banks and to put in place a Prompt Corrective Action 
(PCA) mechanism; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the fresh steps taken for developm ent of a risk profile and designing 
a customary supervisory action plan for each bank? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Risk Based Supervison (RBS) for commercial banks will enhance and 
refine supervisory practices and bring them in line with international best 
practices. The objective of RBS is to ensure stablity of the banking 
123 

RAJYA  SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
system, to promote efficiency, protect the interests of the depositors and prevent 
the misuse of banking system RBS will help Banks in identifying deficiencies in 
systems and controls and to find out appropriate solutions. 
Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) is mechanism based on a pre-
determined rule-based structured early intevention machanism. PCA is 
intended to enhance the effectiveness of the existing supervisory frame-work. It 
has a schedule of corrective action based on three important parameters i.e. 
CRAR, net Non-Performing Assets and Return on Assets, representing capital 
adequacy, asset quality and profitability respectively. Certain trigger points have 
been determined under these parameters and for every trigger point, a set of 
structured and discretionary actions has been proposed, which are designed to 
pre-empt any deterioration in the soundness of banks. 
(c) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has developed a detailed risk profile 
template for compilation of risk profiles of commercial banks under RBS. The 
commercial banks have also been advised by RBI to undertake a self-
assessment of their own risk profiles . A tailor-made supervisory programme 
will be prepared for each bank based on its risk profile.

Royalty on crude Oil 
2779. DR. A.K. PATEL: Will t he Minister of PETROLEUM and 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred Question 
3007 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 18th December, 2001 and state: 
(a) what is the rate of royalty on crude oil and gas in the NELP; 
(b) whether these rates are less than the prevailing royalty rates; 
(c) if so, whether there is any move by the Central Government to 
compensate; and 
(d) what is the lower royalty rates payable to the State Government? 
142 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) As per the provisions of 
the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 and Petroleum and 
Natural Gas Rules, 1959 the royalty on crude oil shall not exceed 20% of the sale 
price at well head and 10% of the value at well head of natural gas obtained by 
lessee. Royalty from offshore areas is paid to the Central Government and from 
onland areas to the concerned State Government. 
Under the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP), royalty rate for 
offshore areas is 10% for both crude oil and natural gas. In case of deep water 
areas (beyond 400 metre isobath), the rate of royalty is 5% for crude oil and 
natural gas for the first seven years from the date of commencement of 
commercial production in the field. For onland area, royalty rate is 12.5% for 
crude oil and 10% for natural gas. 
(b) and (d) The royalty rate for natural gas for onland areas is the same 
i.e. 10% under NELP as well as for the gas producing areas in main of Oil and 
Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd. (OIL), allotted to them on 
nomination basis. Royalty on crude oil prevailing at present is specific @Rs.850 
per metric tonne on adhoc basis w.e.f. 01.12.99. 
(c) The onland blocks under NELP have been offered after obtaining 
concurrence of the concerned State Gove rnment to the fiscal terms of NELP, 
including royalty rates for oil and gas.

Loss due to delay in completion of SSP 
2817. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the delay in Sardar Sarovar Project has 
already cost the nation over Rs. 9,125 crore due to operational cost and 
associated expenses as reported in the 'Assam Tribune' dated the 16th 
September, 2002; 
(b) whether the project was scheduled to be completed by January, 1998 
and it is incurring an average loss of Rs. 5 crore a day since then; and 
(c) the shares of Madhya Pr adesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and 
Rajasthan in the benefits of the multipurpose project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The 
construction of the Sardar Sarovar Dam could not be completed by January, 
1998 as originally planned due to the Writ Petition filed by the Narmada 
Bachao Andolan in the year 1994, the judgement on which was given in 
October, 2000 only. The original estimated cost of the Project as 1986-87 price-
level was Rs. 6406.04 crore, which at 1991-92 price level was Rs. 13,180 crore. 
The estimated cost of the Project at current price-level which is under 
finalisation by the Government of Gujarat is likely to go beyond Rs. 20,000 
crore. Except for a small quantum of water being drawn from the partially 
completed irrigation bye-pass tunnel, no part of the Sardar Sarovar Project can 
be considered as put into operation t ill date. Hence, the question of operational 
cost and associated expenses on the project does not arise. Nevertheless, it 
may be stated that the delay in cons truction of the project has caused the 
nation significant loss on account of project cost escalation, apart from the loss of 
accruable benefits for the period of delay in commissioning different 
components of the project. Thus, the accruable benefits from completed project 
may be considered as likely losses on account of overall delay in construction 
and as per the information made available by the Government of Gujarat such 
annual losses in agricultural production, electricity generation and water supply 
work out to about Rs. 2175 crore, which is equal to a loss of about Rs. 6 crore 
per day.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE : Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving 
me this opportunity to share some of my perceptions in regard to these two 
Bills, the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2001 and the Companies (Second 
Amendment) Bill, 2001. While making his observations, one of my colleagues 
has suggested that there should be a comprehensive company legislation for 
corporate governance. In fact, in the last three or four years, we have 
attempted to do exactly that. One of  the major amendments, which was 
related to the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1997, was done in 
253 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
two stages. Mr. Jaitley was then the Minister - in - charge and I had the 
privilege of presiding ov er the Standing Committee which considered the two 
BilIs. One was, of course, relating to ta king out certain sections to facilitate 
buy-back arrangements and investments in the parent company shares. And 
the other amendment was really very comprehensive. If somebody goes back 
to the history of the Company Laws, he will find that it has almost taken 40 
years to make the major amendments. Fi rst in 1916, thereafter in 1956 and, 
thereafter, initiatives were taken in 1977 and when the legislative process is 
completed through these two Bills, I think this exercise will be over. 
In this connection, I would like to point out that while undertaking the 
major amendments in the Company Law, the question of insolvency and 
winding up, expeditious methods of winding up, also arose. But, at that point of 
time, since the recommendations of the Eradi Committee were not available to 
the Government or to the Standing Comm ittee, it was decided to take it up 
later on. And, in fact, the Government  brought out this piece of amendment 
after the recommendations of the Eradi Committee were available. 
One of the major reasons, which we shall have to keep in view, is 
that why the process of winding up shou ld be expedited. Apart from any other 
things, harassment of the individuals concerned, there are two major aspects 
which sometimes fail to get due attention. First is that the productive assets 
get unlocked and remain unlocked for a very long period of time, if the 
dissolution does not take place expeditiously. Secondly, most of the time, it 
has been found that the assets are frittered away and completely wasted and, 
Sir, if you look at the figures, which are indicated in the report itself, you will be 
astonished to find out that in number of  cases, it has taken 15 years, 20 years 
or 25 years. Now what assets would re main intact for a period of 20 or 25 
years? 
Sir, upto 31st December, 1999, the age-wise classification under 
winding up process has been given. Fo r the o to 5 years, there are 1065 
cases, for 5 to 10 years, there are 603 cases, for 10 to 15 years, there are 482 
cases, for 15-20 years, there are 321 cases, for 20-25 years, there are 251 
cases and for 25 years and above, the figure is 473 cases. The simple point is 
after all that the country has invested a lot in creating certain assets, the 
productive potentiality of which is not being utilised and they just get simply 
wasted. 
254 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Therefore, it was considered nece ssary that expeditious measures 
should be taken. We have discussed on a number of occasions about pending 
cases in the High Court. Special attention cannot be paid by the High Courts to 
dispose of the cases in the winding proc ess despite whatever we may like to 
have, whatever may be our desire. As fa r as the decision of winding up is 
concerned, it was to be decided in thre e compartments, one in the High Court, 
another in the Company Law Board and t he third one in the BIFR, as a last 
resort. But the important aspect of t he BIFR was that their major mandate was 
for the rehabilitation. I am not going in to the aspect of apportioning the blame 
but the fact remains that in a number of  cases which were registered with the 
BIFR, from 1987 to 2000, total number of cases were 3,068 and upto 1999, 
actual revival took place in 264 cases. About 375 cases were in the revival 
process and winding up was recommended in 741 cases. But the pending 
cases were almost more than one-third. It means that no decision was taken. It 
may be that they did not have the m andate, they did not have the teeth or 
whatever be the reason, but the fact remains that the decision could not be 
taken in most of the cases referred to these organisations, and as a result of 
which, large number, even here too, of  productive assets were either not 
utilised or in the process of being wasted. If I could understand it correctly - if I 
am wrong, the hon. Minister may correct  me - the Eradi Committee, an Expert 
Group, was suggested, separately, to prepare a special note in regard to the 
BIFR and as to what could be done. They considered that it would be desirable 
to combine all the three functions in one body so that there is  no multiplicity of 
the organisations and one does not work at cross purposes. In fact, we had - I 
am just telling about the Committee - an  opportunity of listening to a large 
section of the opinion-makers, opinion-builders and opinion-holders in the 
society. It is not that we only listened to the corporate sector. We devoted one 
full day - I hope my colleague, Shri Bhardwaj and other Members of the 
Committee would bear with me -for having an interaction with the trade union 
organisations. All the major Central trade union organisations responded to our 
invitation and they gave their suggestions. It is not that we had agreed to 
everybody's suggestion. We tried to find out how to resolve this problem and in 
what best manner these issues could be  resolved. That is why, we had 
recommended to the Government that this piece of legislation should be 
expedited. I am happy that with the consent of this House we would finally be 
able to pass this Bill. So far as the anom aly which is arising out of SICA is 
concerned, as the  hon.  Minist er has very correctly pointed out,  it  is  not that 
all the 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
provisions of this Amendment Bill wo uld be operationalised on the same day. 
So far as SICA is concerned, the rele vant provisions could be operationalised 
at the appropriate time. I am happy that such a provision has already been 
made in the Bill. I am glad that at the very beginning of the debate, the Finance 
Minister assured us about the continuat ion of employment of those who are 
working in the Company Law Board and other organisations. Of course, 
depending on their eligibility, they can go on deputation. Anyway, nobody is 
going to lose his job. The hon. Minister has already given this assurance. I 
would like to submit one thing for the c onsideration of the hon. Minister. Even 
after the Bill is passed, we shall have to consider very seriously as to how to 
re-address the sickness of industries and arrive at expeditious decisions. To 
my mind, what is important is, if we c an take decisions in time and prevent the 
sickness, the question of rehabilitation would be much easier. As you are 
doing major reforms in the banking sector and the financial sector, with the 
passage of the NPA Bill, the banks would be more accountable because they 
are the first organisation to understand the sickness of any industry from the 
irregular cash flow statement and other relevant documents. If steps could be 
initiated at that stage, perhaps, we woul d be able to resolve the problems at a 
lesser cost and we would be able to solve these problems in a very short time. 
This is one issue which we cannot ig nore because in our country we cannot 
provide social security and we cannot  create jobs as the developed countries 
can. That is why even in the uneconomic  sector, sometimes, continuation of 
employment and retention of employment  becomes necessary, as there is no 
other avenue open. Therefore, I s upport the Companies (Amendment) Bill 
which has been processed through the Parliamentary Standing Committee. 
So far as the second Bill in regard to producer companies is 
concerned, an apprehension was expressed whether through this exercise the 
cooperative movement was going to be a ffected, whether we were interfering 
with the cooperative character of t he organisations. The most important 
feature of this Bill is when we considered, because in our corporate culture, we 
have the concept of public sector companies, private limited companies, 
ownership, partnerships and a new concept of the producer companies having 
the flexibility of the cooperatives, were  thought of. And, many of the leading 
persons of cooperative movements, they wanted that existing cooperative laws 
are throttling the expansion and the deve lopment of the cooperative sector, 
especially the producer cooperative. 
256 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Therefore, an arrangement should be made, and it is optional; it is not 
mandatory. If somebody wants to conver t itself into a producer company, 
option lies with him, and it requires the special majority in the decisionmaking 
process and if they have that, in that pr ocess, if they go in for competition, and 
if they want to go in for competition, def initely they should have the flexibilities 
available to a company under the Companies Act. Because, cooperative laws 
are more restricting, the enormous powe rs which the registrar of cooperatives 
enjoy, and hardly any decision is being taken by the cooperatives themselves. 
And, within that rigid frame, despite the fact that a lot of concessions, in terms 
of money, in terms of liberty and flexib ility of functioning, were given, the 
movement has not attained the desired level. On the other hand, our corporate 
sector ought to face challenges from the different counterparts belonging to 
different countries with the opening up of  the economy. And, if our corporate 
laws are not in tune and they cannot provide adequate flexibility to the 
corporate sectors to be competitive, in cluding the producer companies in the 
cooperative sectors, then ultimately, we  won't be able to survive. Keeping 
these two basic objectives in view, and after a good deal of deliberations, we 
recommended these suggestions, and I am glad that most of the suggestions 
have been accepted by the Government. We understand that sometimes, all 
the suggestions cannot be accepted. Anybody will be quite happy if all the 
recommendations of the Standing Co mmittee are accommodated by the 
Government, but sometimes there are adm inistrative difficulties. But, by and 
large, the spirit of t he recommendations has been incorporated and with the 
passage of this law, I do feel that Indian corporate sector would be placed on a 
level playing field. They will have the opportunities of competing with the 
others and they will not be fettered by the legal framework which stand in the 
way, which stand in the way of the na tural growth and the development of the 
corporate sector, because India's industrialisation, our economic growth, much 
depend on how our corporate sector behav es; how they become competitive; 
how they become transparent; how they  become accountable; and, how the 
equity culture spreads all over the co untry. Almost 40 years ago, it was 
thought of and one organisation, which the other day, we had an opportunity of 
debating here. The whole purpose of UTI was to create equity culture in this 
country, to create awareness in this country. But because of bad management 
of the corporate sector, they failed to inspire confidence in the minds of the 
people, in the minds of the investors. And, many people invested their surplus 
money in dead assets like gold, but not in equity, 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
because they did not have confidence in the equity market. A series of 
measurements and enactments are necessary, and I must say, it cannot be 
'stop and go'. This is a constant exercise . With the changing world, with the 
changing environment within the country, outside the country, we should have 
the flexibility of adjusting our policies, changing our instrumentality to meet the 
requirements of the time. 
With these words, Mr. Chairman, Si r, I support both these Bills and I 
request the House to accept them. As  Chairman of the Standing Committee, I 
do feel, as their representative, I have this privilege of making this 
recommendation.   Thank you.

effective and as modern and world-class system as we, possibly, can. 
Sir, I will very quickly deal with some of the issues that have been 
raised here. Dr. Singhvi is not here. There is no intention of enhancing the 
Cess that has already been listed here. His  second point related to delays. It 
is to avoid delays that time limits hav e been provided at each stage. It is not 
because we want to perpetuate delays and that, indeed, is the purpose of the 
Committee also, and the Committee had gone into it in some detail. 
Shri Prabhakar Reddy asked for supplementing the Cess. It will not 
be possible for the Government to supplement the Cess that has been 
provided.  This is neither possible nor is it a part of the scheme of things. 
The second point that Shri Reddy had was: If SICA is repealed, and if 
the BIFR is abolished, then, what ha ppens to the pending cases before the 
BIFR? I propose to provide for it when th e SICA repeal is done. After it is 
considered by the Standing Committee, if the Standing Committee grants its 
approval for repeal... then in the SICA (Repeal) Bill that scheme sanctioned by 
BIFR will be monitored by the National Company Law Tribunal. All other 
pending cases will abate for the BIFR but will necessarily have to be referred 
to the National Company Law Tribunal as erosion of net worth is exceeding 
100 per cent in these cases, while the th reshold under the new Bill is only 60 
per cent. Further, we will make the rules. My predecessor in the Company Law 
Ministry, a good friend and an eminent lawyer, Shri Arun Jaitely, has drafted 
these two particular pieces of legislation, when he was holding the charge and 
he has very ably provided them. In the rules we will take care and further 
facilitate migration from BIFR to the National Company Law Tribunal. Shri 
Dipankar Mukherjee had said, are we not pre-empting the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee considering the repeal of SICA? I had answered it at that 
very time when the constitutional aspect was made. We are not pre-empting. It 
has been provided in the Bill, that differe nt sections of the legislation can be 
brought into effect from different date s and the provisions relating to powers 
which are currently with the SICA will be brought into effect, only when, and 
after

wish to take a little time to elaborate it, Sir. This is not a debating point. Mr. 
Virumbi had also said so. Not for argument's sake but to reassure hon. 
Members on the question of security of tenure for labour, I would say this. The 
additional points are: to make such person eligible to be appointed as technical 
Member in the National Company Law Tribunal who has been a presiding

knowledge of and experience, which means , directly, from the trade unions, of

provision for them to be part of the Comp any Law Tribunal; labour as creditors,

Rehabilitation Fund will be used only for making interim payment of workmen,

undertaking; then, Sir, fifthly, the Tribunal shall have powers to dispose of the 
assets of a sick company even during the period of inquiry so as to help 
payment to workmen whenever considered necessary. Sixthly, winding up is to 
be taken up, as the hon. Member, Shri Pranab Mukherjee, has mentioned, only 
as a last resort, after efforts at rehabilit ation have failed. And the third point in 
the Statement of Objects and  Reasons clearly states t hat the main objective is 
facilitating or expediting st abilisation, rehabilitation, or  protection of workers'

of it. I would request the hon. Member to assess the finished product, and not

Ash emitted by thermal power stations 
†401. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the likelihood of 
change in local ecology due to the ash emitted by thennal power stations in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the quantity of ash emitted by each Thermal Power Station in the 
country at present; 
(c) the manner in which the ash is being disposed off by these Thermal 
Power Stations in the country at present; and 
(d) the manner in which Government propose to deal with the hazards arising 
from this ash? 
THE f^lNISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes. Sir. 
(b) The quantity of ash emitted by each thermal power station in the 
country during 2000-2001 is given in Statement-I {See below). 
(c) Ash is being generally disposed of in slurry form in Ash ponds. In some 
power stations, dry system of ash collection/disposal is also in place. 
(d) The following measures have been taken to reduce atmospheric 
pollution due to fly ash:- 
(i) New power stations are being fitted with the latest electrostatic 
precipitators having 99.9% efficiency. 
†Orlginal notice of the quostion was received in Hindi.

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2002] 
(ii) The height of chimneys in new stations has been raised so as to reduce 
impact. 
(iii) In older power stations electrostatic precipitators are being 
retrofitted to achieve prescribed norms of emission. 
(iv) Close monitoring of performance with respect to environmental 
norms on emission by power stations and overseen by the State Pollution Control 
Boards/Committee. 
For water discharge from ash ponds following measures have been 
taken:— 
(a) Water quality norms have been notified 
(b) Monitoring of compliance by power stations themselves and 
overseen by the State Pollution Control Boards/Committees 
(c) Re-circulation of ash pond discharge water. 
In addition use of washed coal is being promoted to reduce generation of ash.

Policy on closure of abandoned mines 
*407. SHRIABANI ROY: Will the Minister of COAL AND MINES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government had set up a Committee to suggest changes in the 
policy regarding closure of abandoned mines in the country, in the recent past; 
(b) if so, the details of recommendations made by the Committee; 
 
(c) whether Government have taken any action on those 
recommendations; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL MINES 
(SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Government had constituted a Committee under 
the Chairpersonship of Additional Secretary, Department of Mines 
26 

[18 December. 20021 RAJYA SABHA 
to look into various issues relating to mine closure.The terms of reference of the 
Committee are to review the existing provisions regarding temporary closure of 
mines, abandonment of mines, planned mine closure and their systematic 
rehabilitation and to suggest suitable amendments in the Mineral Concession 
Rules. 1960 {MCR) and Mineral Conservation and Development Rules. 1988 
(MCDR). 
The Committee has not submitted its reports as yet. The Report of the 
Committee shall be considered in the Conference of State Ministers of Mining 
and Geology which is likely to be convened soon. 
SHRl ABANl ROY: Sir, many mining areas were abandoned and not 
decommissioned, reclaimed or rehabilitated. This has resulted in 
unauthorised mining activities, causing social and environment damage to the 
mines and the surrounding areas. I would like to know what the Government 
propose to do in this regard. 
SHRl RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir. I complement hon. Abaniji for 
raising an issue of great importance. Sir, Mineral resources are exhaustible; they are 
not permanent. Today, they are being exploited. But, a time will come when the 
mineral resources will completely get depleted.Therefore, mine planning was held 
to be a component of the existing rules, because we found that the existing rules 
22,23 and 24 of the Mineral (Conservation & Development) Rules are not 
having sufficient teeth. The Mineral Development Advisory Council raised 
this issue, and the consensus emerged that the whole system of mine planning 
has got to be given a detailed consideration. A Committee has also been 
constituted, under the Chairmanship of Additional Secretary. The report is 
expected by the end of December. On the basis of that, the Government will 
take adequate measures so that a comprehensive mine closure plan can form 
part of mine planning itself. 
SHRl ABANl ROY: As you have rightly said, there is no such provision in the 
Rules. So, my question is: Would the Government think of changing the Rules? 
SHRl RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Surely, the moment the 
recommendation comes—as i have stated in the main answer—we will discuss 
the matter in the meeting with the State Ministers of Mines to be held on 22nd 
January, 2003. After the meeting, we will certainly amend the rules.

†*410. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL:†† 
SHRIRAMJETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any assessment has been made by the Government in regard 
to the time taken in adjudication of rape cases after police investigation and 
the beaming in courts, in Delhi; 
(b) if so, the average time taken for investigation in rape cases by police 
during 1999-2000 and 2000-2001; and 
(c) the detail of rape cases that came to light and the details of the cases 
referred to the court during these years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) to (c) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi have not 
made any formal study of the time taken in adjudication of rape cases. However, it 
normally takes the courts 1-4 years to decide such cases. 
The time taken for investigation for rape cases varies from case to case 
depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. However, the average 
time taken by Delhi Policy to complete investigation in such cases reported 
during the last three years and upto 30th November, 2002 was about three 
months. The details regarding the number of rape cases reported to Delhi 
Police during the same period and their present status is indicated in the 
enclosed Statement-1.

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, during the last one year or so, 
we have seen brutalisation of women in public. We have seen a very, very 
unfortunate incident of a mentally challenged minor being raped in a local train in 
Mumbai; we have known the rape case of Khooni Darwaja, where a student 
belonging to the Maulana Azad Medical College, was brutalised; and we find 
that incidents of rape have increased. In fact, in 1977, the figure was 15,300 
odd, and in the year 2000, the figure is over 16,000. So, this is a matter of great 
 concern. The question that I have, through you. Sir, is that, I find that 
in most of these cases, the litigation goes on, the prosecution goes on for 
several years; sometimes, for 4-5 years, and in some instances that I know of, 
for 10 years. Is there any special way of expediting, or maybe, thinking in 
terms of special courts being set up, because, we are dealing with a section of 
population that needs our immediate attention at this point of time? And we need, 
therefore, special ceils, intervention celts, not just in Delhi, where the police has 
set them up, but, they are not activated, but, throughout the country. Instead of 
the victim having to go to the police, it is the police that must go to the victim. 
Would the hon. Minister respond to this query? 
SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO: Sir, this question 
pertains to Delhi. So far as Delhi is concerned, in all the districts, special cells 
have already been constituted. So far as the question of providing justice 
expeditiously is concerned, in the Home Ministry, we have appointed a 
committee, under the chairmanship of Dr. Justice V.S. Malimath, to make 
specific recommendations on simplifying the judicial process and practices and 
making the delivery of justice to the common man closer, faster, uncomplicated 
and also inexpensive. This Committee has already been constituted.

Government have been taking several steps from time to time to boost 
textile and handicraft exports from country including Andhra Pradesh. Some of the 
Important initiatives are; 
(!) The Government has de-reserved the woven segment of readymade garment 
from the SSI sector. It has also raised the SSI investment limit for knitted 
segment to Rs. 5 crores. 
(il) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1.4.1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(iii) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered under 
TUFS, have been extended the facility of accelerated depreciation at 
the rate of 50%. Cost of machinery has also been reduced through Fiscal 
Policy measures. This further encourages modernisation. 
(iv) With a view to encouraging backward integration, the custom duty on 
shuttleless looms has been brought from 15% to 5%. A programme has 
also been announced to induct 50,000 shuttleless looms and to modernise 
2.5 lakh powerlooms-in the decentralised sector by 2004. 
(v) Foreign equity participation upto 100% through automatic route has been 
allowed in the textile sector with a few exceptions. 
(vi) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches and 
Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing.

"Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting focused thrust for 
setting up of apparel manufacturing units of international standards at 
potential growth centres and to give fillip to exports.

scheme 'Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme' (TCIDS)

2002-03 for providing assistance under the scheme.

Floods in Assam 
*418. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of 
HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any permanent plan to protect the State 
of Assam from devastating floods every year; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what are the steps taken so far to prevent frequent floods in Assam? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
{SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) Flood Management being a State subject, the flood 
control schemes are planned, funded and executed by the State Government 
themselves out of their own resources and as per their own priorities. The 
assistance rendered by Central Government is technical, catalytical and 
promotional in nature. 
(b) Government of India has set up Brahmaputra Board under an act 
of Parliament and the Board was given the responsibility for preparation of 
Master Plans for the control of floods and bank erosion and improvement 
of drainage in the Brahmaputra and Barak Valley also giving due regards 
to the development and utilization of the water resources for irrigation, 
hydro-power, navigation and other benefical use. Accordingly the 
Brahmaputra Board has prepared Master Plans for Brahmaputra and Barak 
Valley, which have been sent to the State Government for implementation. 
The Master Plans inter-alia includes short term and long-term measures 
for flood management. To minimize the damages by floods, construction 
of large-scale reservoirs has been recommended in the Master Plan 
prepared by Brahmaputra Board and also the Rashtriya Barh Ayog as 
long-term measures. Implementation of these long term measures may 
take quite some time and therefore till the time the major projects are 
executed the other short term works like bank protection measures, 
drainage development schemes, run-of the river schemes etc. which when 
completed would contribute to the flood management in a short span of 
time are also ki the plan.

(b) Coal is imported by the consumers due to (i) non availability/ 
Inadequate availability of the required quality indigenously, (ii) for use by 
blending with indigenous coal on environmental consideration and (ill) 
considerations of cost. Domestic coal is cheaper at pithead per tonnes basis. 
However, domestic coal becomes uncompetitive .per tonne basis in certain 
littoral areas due to high Railway freight and low heat content of indigenous 
coal. 
(c) Indian coal, in general, by virtue of its drift origin is having high ash 
content as coaly matter is intimately mixed with mineral matter during formation 
stage. Further, reserve of low ash content coking & non-coking coal is very 
limited in India. 
In contrast, mineral matter content in coal from most other coal 
producing countries is low due to in-situ origin of its formation. Hence, the 
imported coal is superior in calorific value and is having low ash content. 
As a consequence, steel/pig iron plants using blast furnace, soda ash 
manufacturers, ferro-alloys industries as well as merchand cokeries are 
importing iow ash coking coal/low ash metallurgical coke (LAMC) since the 
same are not available as per qualitative and quantitative requirements 
indigenously 
Moreover, corex plants and certain captive power plants (like Maico) are 
also importing low ash non-coking coal due to availability of limited quantity 
of superior grade non-coking coal indigenously. 
Some cement plants are also importing non-coking coal on 
considerations of cost-economics and logistics. 
Due to non-availability of sufficient quantity of low ash coking coal, 
integrated steel plants are also importing coking coal in bulk. 
Raw coal offtake in tonnage from CIL has not suffered on account of 
imports and the same has steadily gone up year to year since 1992-93 upto 
current period {barring 1998-99 when there was industrial recession in the 
country).

†2910. SHRIMOTILAL VORA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it Is a fact that the reasons for most of the accidents are over 
speeding, negligence, drunken driving and ignorance about the traffic rules, 
(b) if so, the steps taken by Government to check the same and also to 
create awareness among the people about the traffic rules; and 
(c) the outcomes thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I. D. SWAMI): (a) Various reasons for road accidents in India are: lack 
of traffic discipline on the part of drivers and road users, phenomenal Increase in 
the number of motor vehicles with no corresponding increase in road capacity, 
mixed traffic conditions, over-speedin g, over-loading, drunken driving, 
mechanical defects in vehicles, etc. 
(b) The measures taken broadly are strengthening and widening of roads 
wherever necessary, improvement of road geometries, provision of road signages, 
construction of by-passess, providing training to the drivers particularly in the 
unorganized sector, publicity campaigns for awareness among the road users, 
various enforcement and regulatory measures like checking of overloading, 
checking of valid permit for driving transport vehicles and vehicles carrying 
dangerous and hazardous goods as well as personal vehicles and 
checking/certifying the periodical fitness of the transport/commercial 
vehicles. All these enforcement measures are being executed by the State 
Governments. 
(c) As a result of various road safety measures taken by the Government 
the number of accidents per ten thousand vehicles has declined from 109.87 
during the year 1996 to 80.89 during the year 2000.

Discussion in the WTO meet 
2971. PROR M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the discussions in the WTO, so far, in regard to the 
textiles; 
(b) whether the same proved beneficial or detrimental to our textile 
industries; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) who are our international partners in the field of textiles; 
(e) whether any agreement has been signed with those partners; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANAGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to (c) Doha Ministerial Conference 
mandated an examination by the WTO's Council for Trade in Goods of two 
implementation proposals relating to the Agreement on Taxtiles and Clothing (ATC) 
for recommending appropriate action by 31 st July, 2002. The first 
180 

[18 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
proposal related to calculating the quota levels for small suppliers for the 
remaining years of the ATC using the most favourable methodology 
available in respect of those members under the growth on grow/th 
provisions. Acceptance of the second implementation tirets required members 
to calculate the quota levels for the remaining years of the Agreement as if 
implementation of growth on growth provision for the third stage had been 
advanced to 1st January 2000 instead of 1st January 2002 could lead to an 
increased market access for our textiles and clothing products. India, had 
coordinated its position on the implementation issue on "growth-on-growth" 
with certain other textile exporting countries, including the ITCB member 
countries, and sought a satisfactory resolution of this issue. This was however 
strongly opposed by the United States and certain other restraining countries. 
The issue could therefore not be successfully resolved by 31st July, 2002. 
India has raised the issue of non-adherence to the deadline on this 
implementation issue as mandated by the Doha Ministerial Conference at the 
WTO and various bilateral meetings with major trading countries. 
(d) The USA, EU Member States, U.A.E., Japan, Saudi Arabia, 
Canada, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Australia, etc. are the major international 
partners of our textile goods. 
(e) and (f) Till December 31,1994, the exports of textiles to certain 
developed countries {i.e. US; member countries of EU; Canada) had been 
governed by bilateral textile agreements entered into between India and these 
countries under the aegis of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement (MFA), outside the 
rules of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). With effect from 
January 1,1995, the quantitative restrictions (import quotas) in the bilateral 
agreements under the MFA, are being governed by the Agreement on Textiles 
and Clothing (ATC) contained in the Final Act of the Uruguay Round 
negotiations of the GATT. Presently, our textiles and clothing items face 
restraints in USA, European Union and Canada. As per ATC,"the textile 
quotas would be phased out and textile sector fully integrated into WTO by 1 st 
January, 2005. 
Export of textiles to developed countries 
2972. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has drawn up a plan to open up in a big way the 
textile exports to developed countries; 
181 

RAJYA.SABHA [18 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
 
(c) whether Government is aware that the textile sector has to face a big 
challenge in the international market in the form of trade defence measures 
like anti-dumping and countervailing duties; and 
(d) if so, steps proposed to take care of these measures? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANAGOUDA R. PATH): (a) and (b) Government have 
continuously been taking steps from time to time to boost textile exports In 
international market. Some of the important initiatives taken in recent past 
are: 
(i)  The Government has de-resefved the woven segment of readymade 
garment from the SSI sector. It has also announced the de-
reservation of knitted segment in the Union Budget 2002-03. 
(ii)  The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(ill) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered 
under TUFS, have been extended the facility of accelerated 
depreciation at the rate of 50%. Cost of machinery has also been 
reduced through Fiscal Policy measures. 
(iv)  With a view to encouraging backward integration, the custom duty 
on shuttleless looms has been brought from 15% to 5%. A 
programme has also been announced to induct 50,000 shuttleless 
looms and to modernise 2.5 lakh powerlooms in the decentralised 
sector by 2004. 
(v)  Foreign equity participation upto 100% through automatic route 
has been allowed in the textile sector with a few exceptions. 
 
(vi)  National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches 
and Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of 
textile industry especially apparel in the field of design, 
merchandising and marketing. 
(vii)  The Government has launched a centrally sponsored scheme titled 
"Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting focused thrust for 
setting up.of apparel manufacturing units of international standards at 
potential growth centres and to give fillip to exports. 
162 
 

[18 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, a 
scheme 'Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS) 
has been launched. A provision of Rs.15 crores has been made in the 
B.E. 2002-03 for providing assistance under the scheme. 
(Ix) The Textile Export Promotion Councils are regularly undertaking 
export promotional activities by way of participation in fairs/ 
exhibitions abroad and organising Buyer-Seller Meets in important 
markets. As a part of the efforts to boost textile exports to Latin 
American markets, a mega Textile Trade show was organised under 
the LAC programme. Co-ordinated promotional events are also planned 
under the Focus Africa programme to boost the exports of yarn and 
fabrics to the growing African apparel industry. 
(c) and (d) The textile industry in India is facing certain trade defence 
measures. However, appropriate action is taken by the designated Indian 
authorities under anti-dumping, countervailing and safeguard measures under 
the WTO agreements. As regards the anti-dumping/anti-subsidy action faced by 
Indian exporters, the concerned Export Promotion Councils in consultation with 
the Government of India co-ordinate the defence of Indian exporters. In case of 
any violation of the provisions of the agreement in such investigations, the 
Government takes recourse to the Dispute Settlement provisions of WTO in 
consultation with the industry.

Demand for setting up of pre-cyclone warning system In coastal 
area of Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, Government is fully aware that the 
coastal area of Orissa is the most vulnerable and prone to cyclones. The 1999 
super cyclone had played havoc with the State. Flood and cyclones do not 
come suddenly. They do give some warning. The cyclones can be monitored 
and warning issued in advance to the residents of the coastal areas, to 
minimise loss of life and property, as is the position in USA and China, who 
give some advance warning. Orissa is the poorest, backward, illiterate and 
cash-starved State. They neither have the wherewithal nor the resources for 
developing a pre-warning system or other infrastructure facilities. The State is 
wholly at the mercy of the Centre or international agencies for financial, 
material and other related help. Though belated, I would like to make a humble 
request to the Centre, that they should immediately get in touch with the State 
authorities, formulate short and long-term plans and set up a pre-cyclone-
warning machinery and other related Infrastructure facilities In the coastal 
areas of the State, at the earliest. Any kind of slackness or delay now may cost 
us very heavily, which we may not be able to recoup or recover at a later date.

National curriculum framework for school education 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Sir, the Supreme Court of India 
pronounced its judgement, on the National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education and related issues, on September 12,2002.The three-j udge Bench 
delivered three separate judgements in this case being Write Petition No. 98 of 
2002. The Court reiterated the well-established propositions that it has a 
limited jurisdiction to intervene in the implementation of a policy, that it is not in 
the province of the Court to decide on the good and bad points of an Education 
Policy, and that it is for Parliament to take a view on this subject. Two of the 
learned Judges also directed the Union of India to consider the matter of filling in 
the vacancies in the membership of the Central Advisory Board of Education 
(CABE) and convene a meeting of CABE for seeking its opinion on the policy and 
the curriculum.

vacancies in CABE and convene its meeting expeditiously; (2) to appoint an 
independent body of experts to evaluate the new textbooks in Social Sciences 
and not to introduce them in schools until such evaluation is complete; and (3) to 
obtain parliamentary endorsement of the changes that the Government has made 
and of those it proposes to make in the National Education Policy which was, 
unanimously, approved by Parliament in 1986 and is still in force.

Prevention of use of pesticide by Prawn Mafia in Orissa 
DR. M. N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, through this Special Mention, I wish to draw 
the attention of the Government to the danger that is being posed to environment, 
marine animal-life and human-life in coastal Orissa due to pesticides. 
Of late, a new danger to environment, animai-life and human-life has 
emerged in coastal areas of Orissa because of the use of a powerful pesticide 
by prawn mafias.This pesticide passes under several names like Super-killer, 
Cyber-hit, etc., and Is plentifully available in local markets. Pesticides are 
usually used to kill pests and insects on vegetable plants and crops. But, if 
powerful pesticides, in concentrated does, are released in river-water, 
poisonous water falls into the sea and makes the prawns and other variety of 
fishes benumbed enough to float to the shore in huge quantities and the fish-
mafias collect them easily. This kind of mid-night operation has been detected 
on the great rivers of Orissa like Brahmani, Baltarani, Kashi, Chitrapala and 
Mahanadi. While fresh-water river fishes die or get diseased, river water gets 
polluted. And, the villagers, after their bath in these rivers, develop skin 
diseases. Animals die or suffer from ailments by drinking the river water. It is 
reported that thousands of people suffer from side effects after using the river 
water. Fish merchants earn big profits from unethical activities. They transport 
hundreds of quintals of sea-fish to markets. 
205 

RAJ YA SABHA [18 December, 2002] 
Huge quantities of prawns are sent to fish-processing plants at the Paradip 
Port from where they are exported to distant places and other countries. 
Sir, it is one thing to catch fish by traditional methods for consumption, 
but it is another thing to pollute rivers for catching more fish by wrongful 
methods. I appeal to the Ministry of Environment and Forests to instruct the 
State Government to prevent such an activity, which threatens plant life on the 
river-beds and which also adversely affects the river water. If timely steps are 
not taken, the situation will worsen. 
Request to honour the designer of the national flag of the country, Shri 
PingaliVenkayya 
DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY (Nominated): Mr. Chairman Sir, I seek your 
kind permission to bring to the notice of the House the need for 
commemorating the great services of the designer of our National Flag. The 
National Flag is a symbol of honour and dignity of an independent country. The 
tri-colour was designed by Shri Pingali Venkayya, Andhra Pradesh, in 1921. 
Gandhiji approved it during his visit to Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh. Born on 
2nd August 1878, Shri Venkayya was a great patriot. At the age of nineteen 
years, he went to South Africa, where he met Gandhiji. He fought in the Boer 
War. Shri Venkayya was a person of immense talent. His book "A National 
Flag for India" published in 1916, attracted the attention of several national 
leaders. In his article in 'Young India' dated 13th April, 1921, Gandhiji 
appreciated the efforts of Venkayya in designing a flag for India. Shri Venkayya 
served the country through his efforts in several fields. He was a linguist, with a 
profound knowledge of Japanese, Sanskrit, Urdu, Telugu and English. His 
endeavour in the fields of cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, etc. was remarkable. In 
those days, he served in areas like agriculture, education, metallurgy and 
geology, with devotion. Shri Venkayya died on 15th January, 1963.1 feel that a 
grateful nation should remember the person who designed the National Flag. 
The house in Bhatlapenumarru village of Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, in 
which he lived, is now in a dilapidated and neglected condition. I appeal to the 
Government to take steps for commemoration of the noble memory of this 
great patriot.

Need to enhance baggage allowance to Indian expatriates returning 
home 
SHRI MP. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Sir, I draw the attention 
of the august House to a very serious issue which is being faced by Indians 
employed abroad. They go to foreign countries, leaving their families here, for 
finding some solution to the problem for their sustenance. After working hard there, 
they return to the country by purchasing necessary things for their nearest and 
dearest back home. But, unfortunately, the existing baggage allowance 
permitted to them is only up to Rs. 12,000. The salary of an Indian worker, for 
example, in UAE is estimated approximately at AED1,200.Those employed 
abroad come on vacations only once in every two or three years. Naturally, their 
two or three months' salary will be set apart to buy some necessary things for 
their families, relatives and some gifts for their friends. All these contribute a 
share to their baggage. Unfortunately, the Indian rupee also has devalued 
considerably and it has increased the price level index in economy. So, the limit 
of Rs. 12,000 is a very small amount, as far as the economic condition of 
expatriate passengers is concerned. I, therefore, request the Government to 
enhance the baggage allowance from the present level to a reasonable level. It Is 
to be fixed, at least, equal to three or four times of the average salary of an Indian 
worker in the country where he is employed. Sir, provision can be made for a periodic 
revision of the allowance according to the changes in the economy. The 
enhancement in allowance will smoothen the custom process and will help to 
solve so many problems they face during their journey back to their mother 
country. This will be an act of mercy to Indians working abroad from the 
Government.

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Mr. Chairman, Sir, the 
Fertilisers and Chemical Travancore Ltd., Kochi is the largest GPSU in the 
State of Kerala employing about 6000 employees directly and about 10,000 
person indirect with an annual turnover of nearly Rs. 200 crores. FACT has land 
assets of 2300 acres. The total assets of FACT will not be 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2002] 
less than Rs. 5000 crores. The Government of India has initiated the process 
of disinvestment of FACT in spite of the fact that fertiliser is a core industry of 
India. The present proposal for privatisation of FACT will have to address the 
following issues that the farmers of South India will have no public sector 
company to cater to their needs. FACT is having natural asset, that is, land 
asset of around 2300 acres. The loss of this natural asset will be a big loss to 
the public exchequer. The Government of India is a guarantor for Rs. 400 crores 
OECF loan taken by FACT. If the Government of India is continuing to stand as a 
guarantor or writes off the loan, it is handing over public exchequer's money to 
private parties. If the Government of India can write off the loan now, FACT 
continue to exist as a profitable CPSU. The public sector protection rally at 
Ernakulam on 13th December, 2002 against privatisation has clearly 
demonstrated that the public does not want privatisatin of FACT. 
Therefore, it is urged that the decision to privatise FACT may be 
reviewed and a high powered committee may be appointed to consider the 
revival and restructuring of FACT in public sector.

The Control of National Highways (Land andTraffic) Bill, 2002 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI): Sir, I 
beg to move: 
"That the Bill to provide for control of land within the national Highways, 
right of way and traffic moving on the National Highways and also for 
removal of anauthorised occupation thereon, as passed by Lok 
Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Mr. Chairman, sir, with your permission, I would just give a brief 
synopsis of the Bill. In our country, there is a virtual revolution going on in the road 
sector.This Government has undertaken to improve aout 14,0000 
214 

[18 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
kms. of National highways, to provide money for Improving the State Highways 
and also to provide connectivity to almost over one lakh villages in our country, 
under the Prime Minister's Garmeen Sadak Yojna. During the last tew years since 
the Central Road Fund has come into being, and provision of funds for the 
National Highways Development Project, a tremendous anrount of physical 
progress, on the ground, has already taken place. 
In our country, we have 58,112 kms. of National Highways, out of the 
total road network of 33 lakh kms. on record. But, a large portion of the National 
Highways is under encroachment and unauthorised occupation, with the result that 
whenever we want to improve these roads, we face the problem of evictions, 
court cases, etc. Because of this, apart from excessive expenditure,even the 
timeframe goes completely out of gear. Therefore, it is being though that, at least, 
on the National Highways land, which are owned by the Central Government, we 
should make sure that encroachments do not take place in future; and if they do 
take place, then these are prevented and action taken.The existing encroachments 
on the National Highways are taken care of by certain organisations. Therefore, a 
Highway Administration is proposed to be set up under this Bill. Also, a Tribunal 
is proposed to be constituted under this Bill so that if there are any complaints 
with regard to actions on the part of the Highway Administration, the Tribunal can 
go into the complaints and take a decision. 
With this background, I introduce the Bill. I request this august House to 
kindly consider and pass this Bill. Thank you.

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Madam, National Highways 
are rapidly getting congested and choked by undesirable roadside development and 
encroachment, especially near towns and cities. This not only adds to time, but 
cost also. Hence, there is a need to remove all such encroachments and 
roadside developments without involving long litigations and court cases. 
Infrastructure is very important in country's economic development. Road 
network is an important infrastructure and if neglected, can work as a barrier in 
the way of economic growth. Huge investments can go waste if traffic on National 
Highways gets congested and choked, as a result of narrowing down of roads at 
certain points. The results are; wastage of fuel, reduced speed, high incidence of 
accidents, increased operational cost etc. Today, Highway Authorities do not 
have adequate legal authority to deal with encroachers or digging work on roads by 
municipal corporations. What is required is smooth running highways. The 
present legislation can help a lot in removing obstacles and illegal 
encroachments faced by road users today. f\^adam. the National Highways 
Development Project represents a new road vision for the country. When 
completed it will alter the whole road landscape of the country.The dedicated Central 
Road Fund being financed by a cess of Re. one each in diesel and petrol is 
expected to mobilise Rs. 6,000 crores per annum. This fund should be utilised 
properly. I strongly feel that when a National Highway approaches the towns and 
cities, a by-pass road should be constructed. There are many placed where by-
pass road should be constructed.There are many placed where by-pass roads 
are already there. But at certain placed where there is no by-pass they have to 
be constructed. Also a service road to the villages is very essential. I think this 
will help a lot in smooth flow of traffic. I understand that out of the Central Road 
Fund, 50 per cent is to be spent on rural roads. But I do not know whether it is 
strictly followed or not. How much road length has been constructed in the rural 
areas? How many villages are without all-weather roads? A balanced approach 
towards road development will go a long way in providing better facility and 
ensuring fast movement of both, goods and passenger traffic. 1 would say that a 
monitoring cell to oversee the progress of National Highway Development in 
different States is necessary. It should be ensured that finances are properly 
utilised. Madam, a World Bank Study has estimated an economic benefit of Rs. 
8,000 crores per year on account of Golden Quadrilateral alone. It will generate 
employment of atraut 180 million man-days. Madam, 1 support the legislation, which 
will give power to the Highway Authorities to regulate traffic on National 
Highways. I welcome this Bill. Thank you, Madam.

face. What does that mean? You have got a ten-year Plan. You should start

be rehabilitated, because once they move out, nobody will care for them. So, this 
aspect has to be taken care of well in advance. Prior rehabilitation programmes 
are, therefore, a must. 
The Bill provides for a Highways Administration to be put in place. It 
hasTritxjnals to be put in place. Powers to clear roads have been assumed. These 
are broadly the purposes of this Bill. In this connection, I have a few 
suggestions to make. 
Firstly, the Ministry would be well-advised to pick up from the Geological 
Department, or whichever department it may be, the satellite pictures of the 
places where they are going to build roads, and find out what their condition in 
the monsoon is, so that when the road is actually built, the height is kept at 
such a level that the water does not flow over it. Then, there should be 
breakdown lanes, which are a necessity in the matter of highways.The ravine area 
should be quite broad. In fact, there should be a service road on either side to take 
care of the slow-moving vehicles. There is one problem, and I do not know how it can 
be tackled, that is the movement

of cattle-which takes place in a massive form in this country-on the roads. Perhaps,

sanctuaries. So, what I suggest is, alongside the sanctuaries, regular fences

Madam, the Government is building bypasses on the National 
Highways. These bypasses should be not less than one kilometre away from 
small towns, two-three kilometres away from cities, and five kilometres away from 
big cities. If it is done that way, it is almost certain that the ehtire area will be

be built at various places to connect the cities from different points. So, there 
should be many such bypasses and there should not be any need to go through 
any big city. 
Madam, I find that a huge administrative outgo has been envisaged in the 
Bill. There are tribunals, officials, and a whoJe set-up is there. We have already

one will be able to save Rs. 1 crore, by way of toll collection in just one month. 
So, it is never to expensive to install that kind of a stuff. 
As far as the Tribunal is concerned. I would like to say something. I, could 
not get time, yesterday, to suggest something about the Tribunal to Shri Jaswant

SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN (Assam): Ma dam, it is very difficult to 
express my thoughts within three minutes. In the past I have not taken much time 
of the House and today also I shall not take much time. But please let me 
express what is in my mind. 
Madam, I thank you for giving me this opportunity. National Highways are the 
lifelines of the nation, in addition to Railways' network. So, protection of highways' 
land and other properties related to it. assumes much significance. Secondly, 
due to the ever-increasing traffic on the National Highways, different kinds of 
dangers, including accidents, have also been increasing. So, I thank the hon. 
Minister for bringing this Bill on the control of land and traffic of National 
Highways. 
Madam, in many States, the National Highways are in a very bad shape. 
The National Highways in the North-Eastern States are in a deplorable 
condition, due to recurring floods and other natural calamities of the region like 
landslide, etc. The NH-31 which connects Guwahati with the rest of the country is, 
nowadays, in such a deplorable condition that it is used for traffic with tremendous 
harshrp. Other Highways of the region also are no better than the NH-31. So, 
this creates a lot of difficulties in respect of the supply of essential goods as 
also the development and expansion of commerce In the region. If the Highways 
are in a bad shape in Assam, then all the North-Eastern States, barring Sikkim, 
would suffer. So, repair and improvement of the Highways in the region is very 
essential. 
The establishment of the Highways Administration, as sought by this Bill, 
may be very helpful in this regard. Highways Administration may look into these 
matters. Moreover, as regards the repair and rebuilding of the Highways, 
organizations like the Border Roads Organization, the State PWDs, and the 
CPWD are used. The activities of these organizations should also be 
coordinated. The proper utilization of funds is another problem.The proposed 
Administration must look into this problem as well. 
In Assam, the BRO has been given the authority to rebuild the National 
Highways from Rangia to Dhemaji. This Highway connects Arunachal Pradesh 
also. This Highway ife very badly damaged by the nature and recurring floods 
in the district of Dhemaji. The action on the part of the BRO is very slow now. 
The Minister should look into the matter. 
240 

[18 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Some roads used for commercial purpose, connecting two or more States, 
and for the connectivity of the region with the rest of the country, are very 
essential. Dhodar Ali Road is one such road and it is a historical road; it connects 
a part of Assam, Nagaland and a part of Arunachal Pradesh. This road is to 
be converted into a National Highway. As it connects these states with the 
rest of the country, through NH-37 and NH-31 the conversion should be done 
immediately. The Minister has got this request with him and I urge upon him to 
consider this conversion and announce it within the current Tenth Five Year 
Plan. 
As far as the National Highway-153 is concerned, the Minister has already 
accepted the still-well road as NH-153 and this road is also historical.This road 
goes up to Myanmar and then to China. It is necessary for commercial purposes. I 
thank the Minister for having taken this road as a National Highway and 
Arunachal Pradesh PWD has been given the charge to build this. I thank him for 
that. 
During the implementation of the administrative measures, disputes may 
arise. Hence, the need for Tribunals. The Bill deals with setting up of Tribunals 
exclusively. I support the measures for establishing these Tribunals. 
I request the Minister to look into the matters raised by me, as regards 
the improvement of the National Highways, very urgently; and the conversion of 
Dhodar Ali Road into a Highway may be taken up within the current Five Year 
Plan period. I also support the establishment of the Highways Administration 
and the Tribunals to decide on disputes arising out of the new Highways 
Administration. 
With these words, I support the Bill.
