SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Mid-year Review Of Country's Economy And Its Implications. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Madam, I rise to intiate discussion 
on the mid-year review of the country's economy and its implications. Madam, 
recently, the hon. Finance Minister, or his Ministry, had produced two important 
documents - one was the consultation papers on direct and indirect taxes, and 
other is an authoritative mid-term review of the economy. 
[MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
I commend these intiatives of the hon. Finance Minister. But, having said 
that, it is also odd that soon after the publication of both these documents, 
there were efforts to dilute their impact. The Spokesmen of the ruling party 
debunked some of the recommendations of the Kelkar Committee's Report. The 
hon. Finance Minister, later on, was compelled to say that he did not have any 
intention of taking away some of the tax concessions enjoyed by household, 
particularly, building houses. In the same way, the mid-term review talked in 
terms of rationalising and reprioritisation of the sbusidies. It also talked of 
realignment of the rates of small savings. The very next day, the Finance 
Secretary held a Press conference, saying that the Government had no 
intention of doing any such thing. Well, all this, I think, dilutes all the seriosness of 
this document. 
252 

[18 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
But, that is an aside statement. What does this document review? This 
document, according to the Finance Ministry, reviews the performance of the 
India economy. It reports current developments in the economy, with a particular 
focus on the Central Government finances, so as to facilitate an informed public 
debate on the likely policy options. 
Sir, the first and foremost thing that we would have expected in a review 
of this type is that, some of the burning issues, which face the common man in 
this country, or, for that matter, common woman in this country like, what is 
happening to the state of employment; what is happening, in the same way, to 
those living below the poverty line, their numbers, or what is happening to the 
acute distress faced by farmers in large parts of our country, would be 
addressed. Those things are totally missing from this review. The review talks in 
terms of drought and macro numbers. These are useful, but ultimately, an 
economy is not an end in itself. It does not exist for its own sake. The economy 
is a means to enable our people to lead a life of dignity and self-respect. So, 
things that bother people, I think, should constitute the core element of any 
such review. But, those things, unfortunately, are missing in this document. 
The document talks in terms of the expected growth rate of the economy. 
According to the Government statement, as of now, it appears that the 
economy this year will register an increase in the national income of between 
5 to 5.5 per cent. Sir, there are reasons for this development. Maybe, the 
drought is one such factor. The external situation is also mentioned. But, one 
has to compare the realised growth rate with the targeted growth rate of the 
Tenth Five-Year Plan, and this happens to be the first year of the Tenth Five-Year 
Plan. If we are starting the first year of theTenth Five-Year Plan. If we are starting 
the first year of the Plan with a growth rate of not more than 5 per cent, how are we 
going to achieve 8 per cent growth rate? What policy measures are needed to get 
to that growth rate? Has the Government adopted any of those measures in the 
current year, which, in the next two or three years, will ensure that the economy 
can move on to a higher growth path? I am sorry to say, Sir, that on all these 
matters, the review does not throw much light, and in fact, any discussion on 
what is happening in the current year of the economy, cannot be explained 
away in terms of a drought, nor can it be explained away in terms of what is 
happening to the world economy. But, it must rec ognise that for the last five 
years in a row, both the agricultural growth and the manufacturing growth in this 
country have steeply declined. Sir, I have with me some numbers from the national 
accounts data, which show

Statement 
(a) and (b) Licenses for Cellular Mobile Telephone Service (CMTS) have 
been granted to private operators as a result of tenders received in three phases in 
the year 1992,1995 and 2001. Amendment to the clauses of the License 
Agreement have been carried out from time to time as per the emerging 
requirements. Salient features of the amendments carried out so far are given in 
the Statement-I {See below). 
(c) These amendments to License Agreements have been uniformly applied 
to all the Licenses and therefore, all th e Licensees are beneficiaries; list of 
Licensees indicating the Service Area of each Licensee is at Statement-ll. 
Statement-l 
Salient Features of the Amendments to License Agreement 
(i) By an amendment dated 23.10.1997 transfer or assignment of License 
in accordance with conditions of Tripartite Agreement amongst 
Licensor, Licensee and Lenders,was permitted. This was to facilitate 
financing of projects by the Lenders. 
(ii) By an amendment dated 23.10.1997, the limit on external/ 
international commercial borrowing imposed in the Licence was 
modified to be in accordance with the guidelines issued on the subject 
from time to time by Ministry of Finance, Government of India. 
(ill) By an offer of Migration Package made in July, 1999, the existing 
Licensees were migrated from fixed license fee regime to the revenue 
sharing arrangement under New Telecom Policy, 1999. The main 
features of this Migration are as below: 
(a) The licence period was extended from 10 years to 20 years. 
(b) Change from duopoly to multipoly regime with effect from 
1.8.1999 i.e. the Licensees surrendered their right to operate 
in a duopoly regime (of only two private operators) with the 
condition that any number of additional private 
 operators can be inducted. 
 
8

[19 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) Change from fixed licence fee as committed at the time of 
grant of licences to licence fee as percentage of revenue 
earned. The licence fee at present for category 'A' . 'B' and 'C 
Service Areas is 12%, 10% and 8% of "Adjusted Gross 
Revenue' respectively, inclusive of Universal Service 
Obligation (USO), apart from separate charges for use of 
Wireless Frequency Spectrum. 
(d) Migration Package is deemed as a full and final settlement 
of all disputes whatsoever, upto the cut off date of migration 
irrespective of whether they are related with the Migration 
Package or not. 
(iv) By an Order dated 1.10.1999 the Cellular License was made 
technology-neutral; earlier to this it was mandatory for the 
Licensees to use Global System of Mobile Communications 
(GSM) technology. 
(v) By an amendment dated 25.09.2001 transfer or assignment of 
licence was permitted in the situation of merger of licensee 
companies if approved by a High Court so long as competition is not 
compromised. 
(vi) By an order dated 1.2.2002 allocation of additional specturm 
beyond 6.2 MHz on payment of additional spectrum charges, 
subject to availability of the spectrum and justification, was 
permitted.

(c) Some of the reasons for the shortfall in edible oils are:— 
81 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 December, 2002] 
(i) Crushing of oilseeds namely. Mustard/rapeseed, Groundnut and 
Sesame is reserved under Small Scale Sector and Oilseed Growers' 
Co-operatives.The capacity utilization generally ranges from an average 
of 10% for the ghanis (small-scale sector) to around 30% in case of 
the expellers in the organized sector. 
(11) Unrestricted growth in the industry consequent upon de-licensing of the 
vegetable oil industry. 
(ill) Creation of capacity totally incommensurate with availability of raw 
materials. 
(iv) Obsolete Technology. 
(v) Very low margin because of s tiff competition, inefficiency of 
operations etc. 
(vi) Speculative nature of trade. 
(vii) Mismatch between (low) raw material production and (high) 
processing capacity leading to a situation of too much capacity 
chasing too few raw materials (oilseeds). 
(vlii) Fragmentation of capacities, poor scale economies, large idle 
capacity. 
(ix) High cost of raw material and processing renders products like edible 
and other oils uncompetitive and affects export prospects. 
(x) Low priced imported oils eat into already fragile trade margins on 
domestic oils. 
(xl) No wonder, the processing industry especially oil milling and 
solvent extraction suffers from pervasive sickness, 
(d) The remedial measures taken and efforts made to increase the 
indigenous production of oilseeds and of edible oils include;- 
(i) A Centrally Sponsored Oilseeds Production Programme is 
implemented in 25 States covering 395 selected Districts to increase 
the production of oilseeds edible oils in the country. 
(ii) A Technology Mission on Oilseeds is in place Jo harness appropriate 
production, processing and management technology. 
82 

[19 December. 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(iii) Intensification of research effo rts to increase the production of 
oilseeds. 
(iv) Increasing the areas under non-traditional oilseeds crops, like 
soyabean and sunflower and exploitation of oilseeds of tree and forest 
origin, rice bran etc. 
(v) Setting up of necessary processing and infrastructural facilities to 
keep pace with the production programme of oilseeds. 
(vi) Assistance for oil palm development. 
(vii) Better incentives to producers through fixation of Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) of major oilseeds. 
(viii) Use of indigenous oils in the manufacture of Vanaspati to at least 
25% of the production on a monthly basis is mandatory at present. 
Higher use of expeller mustard oil in the manufacture of Vanaspati upto 
30% has also been allowed. The objective is to incentivise the 
farmers in terms of better returns for their production. 
In order to harmonise the interests of domestic oilseeds growers, 
consumers and processors and to regulate imports of edible oils to the extent

Palfistan 
Pakistan has established an elaborate infrastructure for the recruitment;

Kashmir and other parts of India. Information 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
105

regarding terrorist infrastructure, in  Pakistan and Pakistan controlled 
territories, for support to terrorism is appropriately shared with other 
countries as a part of the global efforts against international terrorism. 
Government are determined and firmly committed to fight terrorism by all 
means until it is decisively crushed. 
Bangladesh 
The Government of India Is aware of the reports that agencies, inimical 
to India's interests, including the ISI, are misusing the territory of Bangladesh 
for their anti-India activities. 
The Government of India has been regularly taking up these security-related 
issues with Bangladesh at different levels through diplomatic channels and 
institutional mechanism existing between the two countries. The Government of 
Bangladesh has assured that it would not allow its territory to be used for 
activities inimical to India's interests. The Bangladesh foreign minister during 
his visit to India on 16-17 June, 2002 has informed of the decision taken at the 
highest level in the Government not to allow presence of Indian insurgents or 
their free movement across the border. 
Myanmar 
The Government is aware of reports that groups and organizations inimical 
to India's interests are misusing the territory of Myanmar for their activities. 
Most of groups are linked to members of North-East insurgent groups. 
There are institutionalized mechanism where two countries interact 
regularly to address issues related to border management. 
Nepal 
Government is concerned about ISI misusing the Nepalese territories and the 
open India-Nepal border for activities inimical to India's interests and is seized 
of the matter. 
There is close cooperation between Nepal and India on the issue of cross 
border terrorism. Both Governments have agreed that they would 
106 

[19 December. 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
not allow their territories to be used for activities inimical to each other. A 
bilateral institutional mechanism has also been evolved which includes a joint 
working group on border management and Home Secretary level talks. The 
special service bureau has been deployed along the border with Nepal to 
strengthen security in the border areas. The extradition arrangements between 
India and Nepal are presently governed by the Treaty of Extradition of 
1953.The Government of India has proposed that the Treaty be updated and has 
handed over to His Majesty's Government of Nepal (HMGN) a model text of an 
updated Extradition Treaty. 
Bhutan 
The presence of ULFA, NDFB and KLO militants on Bhutanese 
territory has been a subject of discussion with the Government of Bhutan. The 
National Assembly of Bhutan adopted a series of Resolutions in 1999, 2000 
and again in 2001 to control this menace. The extradition arrangements 
between India and Bhutan are governed by the Extradition Agreement signed 
between the two countries on May 20, 1997. Under this Agreement, India and 
Bhutan are committed to safeguarding each other's security and stability.

3050. DR. ABRAR AHMED: Will the Minister of LABOU R be pleased

(a) what are the broad features of the National Policy on Child Labour, 1987; 
(b) whether Government propose to up date this policy to make it more 
purposeful; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) to (c) Government has formulated a National Policy 
on Child Labour, 1987 which contains the following main ingredients:— 
• A legislative action plan; 
• Focussing of general development programmes for benefiting child labour 
wherever possible; and 
• Project based plan of action for launching of projects for the welfare of 
working children in areas of high concentration of child labour.

rehabilitating the children withdrawn from employment thereby reducing the 
incidence of child labour. So far, about 1.49 lakh children have been 
rehabilitated and mainstreamed Into formal education system.

Labour (R&A) Act, 1970 in respect of Central Public Sector Undertakings;

others V/s National Union Water Front Workers and others dated 30.8.2001, laid

under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for Central Government

the Central help rendered to bring down this figure? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE tN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATIVASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The Planning Commission, based 
on the recommendations of the Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion 
and Number of Poor (Lakdawala Committee), uses State-specific poverty 
lines in order to estimate the incidence of poverty.These State-wise poverty 
lines are derived from the national level poverty lines, using state-specific 
price indices and inter-state price differentials.The national poverty lines are 
expressed as monthly per capita consumption expenditure of Rs.49.09 in 
rural areas and Rs. 56.64 in urban areas at 1973-74 prices corresponding to a 
basket of goods and services anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie 
requirement of 2400 kcal in rural ar eas and 2100 kcal in urban areas. The 
national poverty line at 1999-2000 prices is monthly per capita consumption 
expenditure of Rs.327.56 in rural areas and Rs.454.11 in urban areas. 
(b)The consumption basket of goods and services is same for all the 
States but this basket is evaluated at States, prices. Because of difference in 
prices of commodities in different States, the poverty lines differ from State 
to State. 
(c)In 1999-2000, the poverty line in rural areas is lowest in Andhra 
Pradesh with Rs. 262.94 per person per month and highest in Kerala with Rs. 
374.79 per person per month; in urban areas, the poverty line is lowest in 
Assam with Rs. 343.99 per person per month and highest in Maharashtra 
with Rs. 539.71 per person per month. 
(d)There is no such proposal at the moment. 
(e)In view of (d) above, does not arise. 
(f) Based on the data from the latest large sample survey of the 55th 
Round on household consumer expenditure conducted by the National

3109. SHRIMATI N.RDURGA: 
SHRIAIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India successfully launched first meteorological satellite into 
orbit; 
(b) if so, the features thereof and the benefits that would accrue to the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Meteorological 
Satellite (METSAT), the recently launched dedicated satellite for meteorology, 
carries a Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR) designed to obtain images of 
the earth in the visible, thermal infrared and water vapour channels of the 
electromagnetic spectrum, enabling continuous, round-the-clock monitoring of 
the weather system. The Data Relay Transponder (DRT) in the satellite 
enables collection of meteorological data from remote and inaccessible areas over 
land.Thus, METSAT provides better data for weather forecasting. 
(c) The achievements of the mission are as follows: 
— The geo-synchronous launch capability of PSLV has been 
successfully demonstrated. 
— For the first time, a dedicated meteorology satellite which 
provides more clear satellite images and data and also 
meteorological data from remote and inaccessible areas, round-the-
clock for weather predictions, has been orbitted. 
Out of many possible approaches, our investigation envisages a lunar 
mission using PSLV through geo-synchronous transfer orbit which has been 
clearly established in PSLV-C4. 
(d) No, Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL (Bihar): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I rise to raise an issue

I just want to state that the disinvestment process involves entering 
into a share purchase agreement with a strategic partner in terms ef which the 
sale price is determined and the ultimate adjustment of finances takes place,

"Even though the strategic control of Paradip Phosphates Limited has been 
handed over to Zuari Moraq Phosphates, which is the strategic partner, the

which the Bill had to be brought before the House. If we do not pass the Bill

That conclusion is, whenever the Parliamentarians handle a problem, which

the public perception about the Members of Parliament and the Members of

Why don't I consider this Bill good enough? During the last several 
years, we have been trying to introduce reforms in the electoral system in a 
piecemeal manner. We don't realise the simple fact that the electoral system, 
which is the core of the parliamentary democracy, is an integrated system. If 
we handle a problem without handling the related problems, it is as good as 
not handling that problem effectively. The piecemeal approach, which had 
been followed during the last 30 years of electoral reforms in our country, has 
landed us in a situation where the whole system has become discredited in the 
eyes of the people and we ourselves realise it. 
A mention has been made by Shri Bhardwaj about the need for a 
comprehensive approach to electoral reforms. It should not mean a committee 
again. So many committees have gone into the electoral reforms issue, 
starting from the Jagannath Rao Committee, the Tarkunde Committee, the 
V.R. Krishna Iyer Committee, the Indrajit Gupta Committee, the 
Venkatachaliah Commission, the Law Commission and the Election 
Commission. We have any number, of good recommendations and 
suggestions emanating from various Committees and Commissions. All that is 
needed is. the will to implement them. If somebody sits down and tries to 
tackle the problem in an integrated, comprehensive manner, a draft Bill can be 
brought before the Parliament any time. 
One argument that has been raised against a comprehensive 
legislation for electoral reforms--l read about this point in certain articles and 
speeches-is that no other advanced democracy has a comprehensive 
legislation covering all aspects of the electoral system or parliamentary 
system. One or two western countries have attempted a few reforms partly, but 
no comprehensive electoral reforms have been attempted. But my point is that 
India, unfortunately, is not in a situation as that of the advanced democracies, 
Our system has failed. Our electoral system has brought us more discredit 
than credit during the last several years. It has been brought out by the Chief 
Election Commission that the Eleventh Lok Sabha had 40 MPs with a criminal 
background. Some people may justify it by saying that they are technical 
offences or they are not serious enough to be called criminal offences. But the 
fact is that 700 MLAs -- I am referring  to that period -- and 40 MPs -- I am 
referring to the Eleventh Lok Sabha --had criminal background. If you say that 
the western countries are not having it. therefore, we cannot go in for it in the 
east, maybe, it is only evading the issue.

May I make some suggestions for the consideration of the hon. 
Minister, through you, Sir? You may take note of the following seven points 
which I am going to make and try to bring a Bill. In my view, if you adopt all 
these seven points, it may satisfy all sections of the people. 
First, defection should instantly result in disqualification, This subject 
has been discussed threadbare in our country and the inevitable last step that 
we have to take is, as I said just now, instant disqualification. Second, there 
has to be a statutory limit of 10 per cent of the strength of the Lower House for 
the size of the Ministry. We try to fight corruption but we forget that defection 
and corruption arise largely because of the anxiety, greed or ambition, 
undisclosed in many cases, of MLAs and legislators. Once they are elected to 
a legislature, they have also the right to sit on the Treasury Benches or to 
become Ministers. Third, no legislator should be appointed - though In the 
States, it has become a common practice - as Chairman of any corporation or 
public sector undertaking, A lot of corruption takes place and a lot of 
malpractice takes place because we accommodate certain people, who cannot 
be accommodated in the Ministry, through chairmanship of corporations or 
public sector undertakings. 
Fourth, if you have a coalition government, there has to be a 
prescribed minimum strength for a coalition partner to have a seat in that 
Government. You can be a member of the coalition or the group, but to 
become a Minister there has to be a minimum number of members in the party. 
There are States in India where a one-member party or a two-member party 
has representation in the Council of Mincters. This has created a vested 
interest in party splitting because to be small in number has become 
advantageous as they get ministership or other positions. Fifth, no political 
party, which does not publish its audited accounts for the knowledge of the 
people, for the information of the f:30ple, should be allowed as a registered 
party. The allocation of symbol is only for registered parties. Every one has to 
submit himself, every party has to submit itself to this bare necessity of having 
to publish audited accounts; the statement of income and expenditure. These 
are the main holes where corruption takes place. I am not talking of the small 
loopholes. We have to plug the big holes. Sixth, affidavit should be filed about 
the assets and liabilities, not merely by the person who has been elected but 
every candidate should be asked to do that.

on the Mid-Year Review of the country's economy and its implications raised 
by Dr. Manmohan Singh on the le"^ December. 2002. Shn Jaswant Singh. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): Madam. I am grateful to the hen. Members for the views 
they have expressed while participating in the discussion, yesterday. 
I do believe that the dajectlve of the Mid-Year Review of the economy 
and the purpose for which I h^d taken the intitiatlve in bring it out for the first 
time Is very effectively served by the fact that there has been a participation of 
so many hon. Members sharing their views in this discussion. Sharing their 
views with us has certainly benefited me, because it was meant to inform the 
House the likely economic policy options t^efore the country. Of course. I 
accept, since It is a brief document, it is not possible for the document to give 
everything that we ordinarily give. It is also a step in the direction of opening 
up the entire Budget-making and making the exercise more and more 
transparent and participatory. The idea, I think, has been served to make our 
policy determination and formulation, as also the monitoring of that, a 
continuous exercise, rather than once-a-year only event that normally takes 
place with the presentation of the Budget. This kind of a status paper on the 
developments in the economy, with particular focus on Central Government, 
for the first half of the financial year, is not the economic review that is 
normally presented before the Annual Budget. It is our experience that review 
coming, as it does, just two or three days before the Budget. It will not enable 
a kind of public debate, or, information that should take place. That was the 
purpose that I had' in my mind in presenting this Review. I do believe that this 
purpose has certainly been served. I accept the fact that a number of hon. 
Members found deficiency and they had critical observations to make. That is 
part of the purpose of the presentation of such a Review. I did not expect any 
unanimous viewpoint, or expression of viewpoint in this regard. But, certainly, 
the debate that followed has, without doubt, benefited me. I will not refer to 
each and ever/ issue that was raised. But, on certain aspects, for example, the 
hon. Leader of the Opposition. Dr. Manmohan Singh, had certain critical 
observations to make.    He cited one particular 
269 

RAJYA SABHA (19 December. 2002] 
example that, in the Review, you speak of rationalisation of pension, and the 
very next day, the spokesman, I think, the Finance Secretary, had said that 
there is no proposal to bring dovjn any interest rates in that regard. But that is 
the point. I think, both are equally valid observations t>ecause governance is, 
after all, a question of finding the correct balance between two equally just and 
valid concerns. I am sure, the Leader of the Opposition will accept that a 
rationalisation of the Centre's pensions, be they in the pension scheme of the 
Armed Forces, or, of the Central Services, is a very important part of the entire 
reform progress. If we do not address ourselves to the rationalisation of 
pension, in the absence of effective pension funds, in the absence of 
contributory pension scheme, we have a situation, for example, in the Armed 
Forces when we will have a pension bill la rger than the salary bill. Therefore, 
there is a need to rationalise the sole process. The rationalisation of the 
pension process can, by no stretch of imagination, be equated with an equally 
valid concern. It means that those who are pensioners, those who are retired, 
those who are senior citizens, widows, had placed their funds in a kind of 
secured deposits, or secured investments. They must contribute to receive a 
return upon their investments, which is commensurate with what they had 
been getting earlier. That is the essential point. The balancing of these two 
equally valid but competing concerns is, after all, a part of governance and that 
is what the Finance Ministry is endeavouring to do. I sought this only to point 
out that in a continental-sized economy, the complexity of a Federal 
Government, and the managing of this continental-sized economy with 
diversity of it, can simply not be fitted into a pattern which answers to straight 
classifications. That is why, I am entirely in agreement with hon. Dr. P.O. 
Alexander. When we are talking of the nature of India's economy, I think, the 
debate also went into it. The Indian economy can be managed only in the 
manner that our genius enables us to manage. It will not fit into the pattern of 
any standard Western model, It is Indian. We will have to find our answers to 
it. Whether you call it 'mixed economy', or whatever term you like to give it, it 
cannot emulate, and it shall not emulate that; the answers will have to be 
Indian. That is absolutely self-evident; it cannot be anything else. Therefore, in 
this globalizing world, what role does a State have to play? The State 
continues to have a role to play. The State is the sovereign risk taker, the 
ultimate risk taker, and shall have to continue to do it. There are functions that 
only a State can perform, and the State will have to continue to perform. For 
example, in the absence of a welfare net, the obligations of the State such as 
development of social infrastructure, be it 
270 

[19 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
health or education or the amount that the State of India incurs even in regard 
to habitation, carinot be taken up by anybody else. Therefore, the 
management of the Indian economy is always a challenging complex mix of 
both the State-managed economy, and a private enterprise. It is not laissez 
faire, it is not a free-for-all; it simply cannot be, But the creative demand of 
India, the product of genius of India, must be able to flower. That is the 
essence of it. 
Now, there was a question that was put by the hon. Leader of the 
Opposition -- and I am mindful that I have to finish it in time -- that related 
essentially to Value Added Tax and Service Tax, He voiced an apprehension 
that if this was done too quickly, it could result in disruption, and therefore, 
there ought to be a white paper on it. I wish to share with him that we had 
appointed -- I had myself participated in that -- a high power committee, which

from all sides. Just yesterday, the Cabinet has granted its approval to the 
constitutional amendment, which relates to the introduction of Service Tax. For 
example, the National Development Council is meeting on Saturday. I will be 
sharing the text of this constitutional amendment with all the Chief Ministers of 
the States. This will be given to all the Chief Ministers, and it is very closely 
linked to the introduction of Service Tax in the country. Aso, I am sure, the 
hon. Leader of the Opposition, more than anybody else, understands the 
centrality of Service Tax, So far as Value Added Tax is concerned, a number 
of States have already enacted it, and the State Legislatures have taken those 
measures to introduce Value Added Tax. On the 1^' of April, we will have a 
most extensive consultation, I have already worked out a formula, which I have 
shared with the States, and which I will be sharing in more detail with the 
States, to compensate whatever losses that could take place with the State 
finance, not simply for the first year, but for the first three years. That formula 
has been found out and it has found favour with the States. We will share the 
text of the constitutional amendment with the States, and I will have no 
difficulty in sending in advance the Bill to be introduced. 1 do express the hope 
that I will be able to introduce, at least, the constitutional amendment in this 
very august House. The Cabinet approved the constitutional amendment only 
last night. 1 don't want to rush it. 1 will share it with the National Development

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
CH's suggestions on drought 
*441.   SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA:t 
SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Confederation of Indian Industry (Cll) has suggested a series 
of short and long term measures, to help the States cope up with drought in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the response of Government on these suggestions? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Confederation of Indian Industry (Cll) had put a number of 
short and long term measures to deal with droughts and for conservation of water 
generally on its web-site in August, 2002, a copy of which was also made 
available to the Government. 
The short term measures include resort to short duration crops with seed 
subsidy, Food for Work Programme, setting up of State Level Task Forces, 
discontinuance of subsidy on power in Blocks with serious water 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Rumandla 
Raamachandrayya. 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
scarcity, provision of uniform power for water supply, banning of inter-State 
movement of fodder and opening of goshalas, etc. 
The long term measures essentially consist of a number of proposals for 
economizing water use and technological innovations in utilization of water. 
The other measures include sustainable land use through planting of forage crops 
and trees. 
The above constitute well-known strategies of managing droughts and 
ensuring sustainable development. It appears that these suggestions are being 
taken up by the Cll in its interactions with the State Governments. The suggestions 
of Cll have also been referred to the Central Government Ministries/Departments 
concerned with the relevant subject matters. The suggestion regarding banning of 
infer-State movement of fodder, however, may not benefit the acutely drought 
affected States.

Johannesburg Summit on biodiversity sharing 
*442.   MISS MABEL REBELLO.t 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether India participated in the Summit on biodiversity sharing and 
water, sanitation access, held in Johannesburg; 
(b) if so, the plans formulated on the subject in the Summit; and 
(c) the issues which the Indian delegation managed to press? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Miss Mabel Rebello. 
4 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Statement 
(a) The Indian Delegation participated in the World Summit on Sustainable 
Development (WSSD) held in Johannesburg, which considered various issues 
related to poverty eradication, changing unsustainable patterns of 
consumption and production, protecting and managing the natural resource 
base of economic and social development, impact of globalization, health and 
sustainable development and means of implementation. The Summit inter-
alia, emphasized the role of partnerships between Government, business and 
civil society in implementing various outcomes. 
(b) Salient features of Johannesburg Plan of Implementation are annexed 
as Statement-I (See below). 
(c) India through the Group of G-77 and China voiced concerns of 
developing countries to reaffirm the principle of common but differentiated 
responsibilities, ensuring implementation of millennium development goals in a 
time bound manner including access to water, sanitation, energy and health 
services, halting and preventing loss of biodiversity. The efforts made by 
various blocks on imposing disguised trade barriers by way of eco-labelling, 
life-cycle analysis criterion, and inclusion of core labour standards of ILO 
were successfully countered by developing countries. 
Statement-I 
Salient Features of Johannesburg Plan of Implementation 
The Plan of Implementation emerged after WSSD is by and large, a 
compilation of various agreements in terms of reiteration of millennium 
developmental goals (additionality in terms of targets on sanitation), 
reaffirmation of the contents of most of the multilateral environmental 
agreements on biodiversity, desertification, and Ozone depleting substances 
etc. There was no visible progress in so far as Kyoto Protocol on Climate 
Change was concerned. The litmus test of this Plan of Implementation lies in 
its actual implementation by the international community. Salient features of 
Johannesburg Plan of Implementation are as follows: 
Poverty Eradication 
Halve, by the year 2015, the proportion of the world's people whose 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
income is less than $1 a day and the proportion of people who suffer from 
hunger (reaffirmation of Millennium Development Goals). 
By 2020, achieve a significant improvement in the lives of at least 100 
million slum dwellers, as proposed in the "Cities without slums" initiative 
(reaffirmation of Millennium Development Goal). 
Establish a world solidarity fund to eradicate poverty and to promote social 
and human development in*he developing countries. 
Water and Sanitation 
Halve, by the year 2015, the proportion of people without access to safe 
drinking water (reaffirmation of Millennium Development Goal). 
Halve, by the year 2015, the proportion of people who do not have access 
to basic sanitation. 
Sustainable Production and Consumption 
Encourage and promote the development of a 10-year framework of 
programmes to accelerate the shift towards sustainable consumption and 
production. 
Energy 
Renewable energy 
Diversify energy supply and substantially increase the global share of 
renewable energy sources in order to increase its contribution to total energy 
supply. 
Access to Energy 
Improve access to reliable, affordable, economically viable, socially 
acceptable and environmentally sound energy services and resources, 
sufficient to achieve the Millennium Development Goals, including the goal 
of halving the proportion of people in poverty by 2015. 
Energy Markets 
Remove market distortions including the restructuring of taxes and the 
phasing out of harmful subsidies. 
Support efforts to improve the functioning, transparency and information 
6 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
about energy markets with respect to both supply and demand, with the aim of 
achieving greater stability and to ensure consumer access to energy services. 
Energy efficiency 
Establish domestic programmes for energy efficiency with the support of the 
international community. Accelerate the development and dissemination of 
energy efficiency and energy conservation technologies, including the promotion 
of research and development. 
Chemicals 
Aim, by 2020, to use and produce chemicals in ways that do not lead to 
significant adverse effects on human health and the environment. 
Renew the commitment to the sound management of chemicals and of 
hazardous wastes throughout their life cycle. 
Promote the ratification and implementation of relevant international 
instruments on chemicals and hazardous waste, including the Rotterdam 
Convention so that it can enter into force by 2003 and the Stockholm 
Convention so that it can enter into force by 2004. 
Further develop a strategic approach to international chemicals 
management, based on the Bahia Declaration and Priorities for Action 
beyond 2000, by 2005 
Encourage countries to implement the new globally harmonized system for the 
classification and labelling of chemicals as soon as possible, with a view to 
having the system fully operational by 2008. 
Management of the natural resource base 
Water 
Develop integrated water resources management and water efficiency plans 
by 2005. 
Oceans and fisheries 
Encourage the application by 2010 of the ecosystem approach for the 
sustainable development of the oceans. 
On an urgent basis and where possible by 2015, maintain or restore 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
depleted fish stocks to levels that can produce the maximum sustainable yield. 
Put into effect the FAO international plans of action by the agreed dates: 
— for the management of fishing capacity by 2005; and 
— to prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing 
by 2004. 
Develop and facilitate the use of diverse approaches and tools, including 
the ecosystem approach, the elimination of destructive fishing practices, the 
establishment of marine protected areas consistent with international law and 
based on scientific information, including representative networks by 2012. 
Establish by 2004 a regular process under the United Nations for global 
reporting and assessment of the state of the marine environment. 
Eliminate subsidies that contribute to illegal, unreported and unregulated 
fishing and to over-capacity. 
Atmosphere 
Facilitate implementation of the Montreal Protocol on Substances that 
Deplete the Ozone Layer by ensuring adequate replenishment of its fund by 
2003/2005. 
Improve access by developing countries to alternatives to ozone-depleting 
substances by 2010, and assist them in complying with the phase-out 
schedule under the Montreal Protocol. 
Biodiversity 
Achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the current rate of loss of 
biological diversity. 
Forests. 
Accelerate implementation of the IPF/IFF proposals for action by countries 
and by the Collaborative Partnership on Forests, and intensify efforts on 
reporting to the United Nations Forum on Forests, to contribute to an assessment 
of progress in 2005.

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Corporate responsibility 
Actively promote corporate responsibility and accountability, including 
through the full development and effective implementation of 
intergovernmental agreements and measures, international initiatives and public-
private partnerships, and appropriate national regulations. 
Health 
Enhance health education with the objective of achieving improved health 
literacy on a global basis by 2010. 
Reduce, by 2015, mortality rates for infants and children under 5 by two 
thirds, and maternal mortality rates by three-quarters, of the prevailing rate in 200 
{reaffirmation of Millennium Development Goaf). 
Reduce HIV prevalence among young men and women aged 15-24 by 25 per 
cent in the most affected countries by 2005 and globally by 2010, as well as 
combat malaria, tuberculosis and other diseases (reaffirmation of General 
Assembly resolution). 
Sustainable development of small island developing States 
Undertake initiatives by 2004 aimed at implementing the Global 
Programme of action for the protection of the marine environment from land-
based activities to reduce, prevent and control waste and pollution and their 
health-related impacts. 
Develop community-based initiatives on sustainable tourism by 2004. 
Support the availability of adequate, affordable and environmentally sound 
energy services for the sustainable development of small island developing 
States, including through strengthening efforts on energy supply and services by 
2004. 
Review implementation of the Barbados Programme of action for the 
sustainable development of small island developing states in 2004. 
Sustainable development for Africa 
Improve sustainable agricultural productivity and food security in 
accordance with the Millennium Development Goals, in particular to halve 
by 2015 the proportion of people who suffer from hunger. 
9 

RAJYA  SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
Support African countries in developing and implementing food security 
strategies by 2005. 
Support Africa's efforts to implement NEPAD objectives on energy, 
which seek to secure access for at least 35 per cent of the African population 
within 20 years, especially in rural areas. 
Means of implementation 
Ensure that, by 2015, all children will be able to complete a full course of 
primary schooling and that girls and boys will have equal access to levels of 
education relevant to national needs (reaffirmation of Millennium Development 
Goat). 
Eliminate gender disparity in primary and secondary education by 2005 
{reaffirmation of Dakar Framework for Action on Education for Alt). 
Recommend to the UN General Assembly that it consider adopting a decade 
of education for sustainable development, starting in 2005. 
Institutional Framework for sustainable development 
Adopt new measures to strengthen institutional arrangements for 
sustainable development at international, regional and national levels. 
Enhance the role of the Commission on Sustainable Development, 
including through reviewing and monitoring progress in the implementation of 
Agenda 21 and fostering coherence of implementation, initiatives and 
partnerships. 
Facilitate and promote the integration of the environmental, social and 
economic dimensions of sustainable development into the work programmes 
UN regional commissions. 
Establish an effective, transparent and regular inter-agency coordination 
mechanism on ocean and coastal issues within the United Nations system. 
Take immediate steps to make progress in the formulation and elaboration 
of national strategies for sustainable development and begin their 
implementation by 2005.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Government has enacted the Environment (Protection) Act, 
1986 and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 to take effective, measures for 
protection of environment and prevention of ecological degradation in the 
country. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests has brought out a notification vide 
S.0.319(E) dated 07.05.1992 under secti on 3(1) and section 3(2) (v) of the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 prohibiting certain activities in specified 
areas of Aravalli Range in Gurgaon district of Haryana and Alwar district of 
Rajasthan except with the prior permission of the Ministry. The activities covered 
under the notification are (i) location of any new industry including 
expansion and modernatisation, (ii) all new mining operations including 
renewal of mining leases, (iii) existing mining leases in Sanctuaries/National 
Parks and areas covered under Project Tiger and/ or mining being done without 
the permission of the competent authority, (iv) cutting of trees, (v) construction 
of any clusters of dwelling units, farm houses, sheds, community centres, 
information centres and any activity connected with such construction 
(including roads, a part of infrastructure relating thereto) and (vi) 
electrification (laying of new transmission lines). 
The powers of the Central Government under the Aravalli Notification, 1992 
were subsequently delegated to the State Governments of Haryana and Rajasthan 
vide Notification S.0.1189 (E) dated 29.11.1999. Inter-alia, the State 
Governments of Haryana and Rajasthan have been required to draw up master 
plans for development of the area covered by the Aravalli Notification, 1992 
integrating environmental concerns and keeping in view the future land use of 
the area. 
The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has notified Gurgaon town 
and adjoining industrial areas of Gurgaon district, Haryana for regulation of 
ground water development and management on account of depletion of ground 
water due to over-exploitation and deterioration in ground water quality. 
Considering the ecological importance of the ridge, which forms a part

KVKs in States 
*447.  SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY;† 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the objectives and guidelines for establishment of Krishi Vigyan 
Kendras in States; 
(b) the number of such Centres established so far, State-wise; 
(c) whether proposals have been received for establishment of such Centres in 
the newly created States and districts; and 
(d) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The objective for establishment of Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) 
is to provide vocational education in agriculture and allied areas. 
The activities include training of farmers to update their knowledge and 
skills, training of extension personnel to orient them in the frontier areas of 
technology development, on-farm trials to identify the location specificity of 
technology, and frontline demonstration to establish the production potential on 
the farmer's fields. 
The guidelines for establishment of KVK include availability of adequate 
land, capacity of the host institution to provide technology backstopping, 
willingness of the host institution to share its resources, and commitment of the 
host institution to run the KVK strictly on its principles, design, methodology and 
objectives. 
(b) So far 286 KVKs have been sanctioned, besides strengthening of 53 
Zonal Agricultural Research Stations (ZARS) to take up the additional functions 
of KVKs. The State-wise details are given in Statement-I. (See below) 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Out of 47 districts in the newly created States, viz., 
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttaranchal; 16 districts have been

for starting them we need, at least, 50 acres of land; people have to be hired, and

working as Krishi Vigyan Kendras. 
SHRI JAN ARDHANA POOJARY: Out of 286, how many are not functional? 
SHRI AJIT SINGH: Out of 286 Kendras, only 25 Kendras have been 
sanctioned this year. But I dont have the details of the number of Kendras which 
have started functioning. I can admit that out of these 25 Kendras also, there are 
some Kendras, which have not started functioning yet, because they were 
only sanctioned about six months ago.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir.The National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) has 
been introduced in the country from Rabi 1999-2000 season. The salient 
features of the scheme are given in the Statement-I. (See below) 
(c) A Statement-ll indicating district-wise number of farmers benefited in

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
Statement-I 
Salient Features of National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) 
- Scheme is available to all farmers—loanee and non-loanee both-
irrespective of their size of holding. 
- Compulsory for loanee farmers and optional for non-loanee farmers. 
- The scheme is voluntary for the States/UTs. 
- Sum-insured may extend to the value of threshold yield of the area 
insured. 
- Coverage of all food crops (cereals, millets & pulses), oilseeds and annual 
commercial/horticultural crops in respect of which past yield data is 
available for adequate number of years. 
- Among the annual commercial/horticultural crops, eleven crops namely 
cotton, sugarcane, potato, chillies, ginger, onion, turmeric, jute, tapioca, 
annual banana and pineapple are presently covered. 
- Basically all-risk insurance scheme covering all yield losses due to 
natural, non-preventable risks. 
- Premium rates are 3.5% for bajra and oilseeds, and 2.5% for other Kharif 
crops; 1.5% for wheat, and 2% for other rabi crops. In case the rates 
worked out on the basis of actuarial data are less than the prescribed 
premium rate, the lower rate will be applicable. 
- In case of annual commercial/horticultural crops, actuarial rates are 
charged. 
- Small and marginal farmers are provided subsidy of 50% of the 
premium charged from them. The subsidy will be phased out over a period 
of 5 years en sunset basis. 
- To implement NAIS at lower unit of insurance i.e. Gram Panchayat within 
three years. 
- It is proposed to set up a separate agency for implementation of 
NAIS.

SHRI RAM-JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Co-operative Sector plays leading role in the following economic 
areas:— 
(i) Disbursement of agricultural credit; 
(ii) Procurement and disbursement of agricultural inputs like fertilizer, seed, 
pesticides etc.; 
(iii) Marketing of consumer goods; 
(iv) Production and processing of sugar and oilseeds; 
(v) Procurement and marketing of cotton; 
(vi) Milk procurement and processing of milk products; 
(vii) Development and marketing of fisheries; 
(viii) Generation of employment in rural areas. 
(c) Government of India has formulated the following plans to encourage 
the co-operative sector: - 
(i) Co-operative Reforms: The Central Government has enacted the 
new Multi State Co-operative Societies (MSCS) Act, 2002 which 
aims at providing full functional autonomy and democratic 
management to the societies. It has also formulated a Na-ional Policy 
on Co-operatives in consultation with the State Governments. The 
Government is now pursuing v/ith the State

(b) The Policy seeks to actualize the vast untapped growth potential

food and nutritional security, secure a fa ir standard of living for the farmers

environmentally non-degrading and socially acceptable use of the country's natural

per annum in the agriculture sector in a longterm perspective. 
The Policy outlines a nine-pronged strategy such as development of 
sustainable agriculture, food and nutritional security, generation and transfer 
of technology, improving management of inputs, providing incentives for

structure to channelise the energies of small and marginal farmers, ensuring

3137. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN:Will the Minister of

population growth, in the country;

first time, after independence;

godowns, free of cost to the poor, to prevent starvation death incidents;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYANYADAV): (a)The compound growth rate of 
production of foodgrains for the period 1990-91 to 1999-2000 is 1.94% as 
against the average annual exponential growth rate of population of 1.93% 
(provisional) for the decade ending 2001. 
77 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
(b) and (c) The Production of foodgrains in the country since independence 
shows a long-term upward trend, albeit with fluctuations due to variations in 
agro-climatic conditions. The food grains production upto the sixties grew 
mainly due to expansion of cultivated area. After the sixties, the growth was 
mainly due to accelerated rate of productivity. However, lately the cultivated area 
has remained more or less static, and the increase in productivity is not as 
significant as in the seventies and the eighties.Thus, while the overall production 
of foodgrains in the country still shows an upward trend, the rate of growth is 
not as high as it was in the earlier period. 
(d) There is no proposal to distribute foodgrains free of cost. The 
foodgrains under special component of Sampoorna Gramin RojgarYojana (SGRY) 
are supplied to State Governments at free of cost but the Ministry of Rural 
Development re-imburses to Food Corporation of India (FCI) at economic cost. 
So far a quantity of 38.29 lakh tonnes of foodgrains have been allocated to 12 
drought affected States. 
(e) and (f) The storage capacity available with FCI in the State of Kerala 
as on 31st October, 2002 is 6.02 lakh metric tonnes whereas the stock of 
foodgrains on that date was 4.26 lakh metric tonnes. Thus, position of storage 
capacity is comfortable. The utilisation of existing FCI godowns in Kerala is 71 
%.There is still space to store more foodgrains.

Farmers conditions 
3139. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has emerged as an agriculture power, but 
most of the farmers continue to live in pathetic conditions; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that though agriculture is the backbone of our 
economy, much more remains to be done, to improve the lot of farmers; 
(c) if so, the steps being taken in this regard; 
(d) whether new farm pricing model and reforms in farms sector can 
improve that lot of farmers to certain extent; and 
(e) if so, the steps proposed to be taken in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) As per the FAO 
Production Year Book, 2000, India ranks second after China in foodgrains 
Production in the World. India's foodgrains production increased from 50.82 
million tonnes in 1950-51 to 211.32 million tonnes in 2001 -02. This has enabled 
India to become a net exporter of foodgrains. As per the 1990-91 agricultural 
census, there are about 107 million operational holdings (farmers) in India. 
Of them, nearly 60 per cent are marginal farmers with less than 1 hectare of 
land, while about 19 per cent are small farmers with 1 to 2 hectares of land. 
About 13 per cent are in the semi-medium category with 2 to 4 hectares of 
land while those in the medium category with 4 to 10 hectares of land constitute 
about 7 per cent 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
of the total number of farmers in the country. Large farmers with 10 hectares 
and above constitute hardly 2 per cent of the total number of farmers in the 
country. The steps taken by the Government to improve the conditions of 
farmers include special concession/subsidies to small and marginal farmers 
under various schemes like Integrated Cereal Development Programme for 
Rice, Wheat % Coarse Cereals, which have since been subsumed under the 
macro-management scheme so as to give flexibility to States to take up 
activities as per local requirements. 
(d) and (e)The National Agricultural Policy has underscored the need for 
ensuring remunerative prices for agricultural produce through the 
announcement of Minimum Support Price (MSPs) for major agricultural 
commodities. In keeping with this commitment, the Government have been 
announcing MSPs for kharif and rabi crops. In order to compensate the farmers 
for the losses suffered in unirrigated areas and the additional expenditure 
incurred in irrigated areas on account of severe drought this year, the Government 
also announced a special drought relief price ranging from Rs. 5 to Rs. 20 per 
quintal for the kharif crops of 2002-03 season.

(SHRI HUKUMDEO YADAV): (a) to (d) The news article referred to the 
consultations the Government of India had with the Governments of 
States/UTs and with other stake holders on 23rd, 24th and 29th of October, 2002. 
Article 20 the WorldTrade Organisation 's Agreement on Agriculture (AoA), 
provides for commencement of negotiations from 1st January, 2000, in order 
to continue the reform process initiated with the coming into force of AoA 
with effect from 1 st January, 1995, with the objective of establishing a fair and 
market oriented agricultural trading system. However, due to continued high 
levels of domestic support and export subsidies in developed countries, tariff 
and non-tariff barriers andTRQs on products of export interest to developing 
countries like India, meaningful market access has been denied to developing 
countries and international prices for agricultural commodities remain depressed. 
In the negotiations, India has sought substantial reduction of all forms of trade 
distorting domestic support by developed countries, elimination of export 
subsidies other than marketing and transport support provided by developing 
countries for exports, and substantial improvements in market access in 
products of export interest to developing countries. India has also proposed 
that food and livelihood concerns of developing countries should be protected. 
The negotiations are scheduled to be concluded before 1-1-2005.

Guidelines for direct funding by NCDC 
A. CRITERIA FOR DIRECT FUNDING: 
1. Eligibility criteria: 
(i) NCDC may extent direct assistance to existing cooperative societies in operation for 
not less than three years. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
(ii) Routing of NCDC assistance will be as follows: 
(a) Projects of Rs. 10 lakhs and above but not exceeding Rs. 5 crores, 
subject to the eligibility criteria, may be considered for direct 
funding. 
(b) NCDC assistance other than (a) above would continue to be routed 
through State Governments or directly against Government 
guarantees. Even with regard to (a) above, the assistance may be 
routed through the State Government or directly against 
Government guarantee at the willingness of the State 
Government. 
(c) In exceptional cases, for the cooperatives which are financially very 
strong, have good track record of operations and credit 
worthiness, projects above Rs. 5 crores (including working 
capital loan) may be considered for direct funding with the 
approval of the Board. 
(d) Multi-state cooperatives would continue to be assisted directly, 
subject to the eligibility criteria, irrespective of the amount 
involved. 
(iii) The society should have positive net-worth, not less than 100% of paid-
up share capital i.e. there should be no erosion in the paid-up share 
capital. 
(iv) The society should not have any cash losses during last three years and 
there should be net profit in at least two of previous three years. 
(v) The debt equity ratio will normally be 65:35, depending on economic 
viability of the project. 
(vi) Value of assets to be mortgaged to NCDC as security against the loans 
should have adequate security margin, normally not less than 1.5 times. 
(Shortfall in the security may be made good by way of guarantee of a 
scheduled bank or. an FDR endorsed in favour of NCDC). 
(vii) Working capital loans to cooperative societies/federations may be 
secured by hypothecation of stocks/debtors/other assets, keeping a 
minimum margin of 20%. If considered necessary, NCDC may 
94 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
ask for additional security of first or second charge on the fixed assets. 
(viii) If considered necessary, the society may be asked to open an Escrow 
account with a scheduled bank/state coop, bank/distt. coop, bank in which 
part of sale proceeds will be deposited for servicing NCDC loan. In case 
Escrow account is opened with a distt. coop, bank, its financial position 
may be ascertained. 
(ix) Audit of accounts should be complete upto previous year within 6 
months of close of the financial year. In cases where audit is undertaken 
by Government auditors and it is not complete, in such cases accounts 
audited by Chartered Accountant's firm will be submitted. 
(x) The society seeking NCDC assistance, or any other society on which 
directors of this society have been directors, should not have any major 
default in repayment of loans to NCDC/banks/financial institutions. 
(xi) NCDC, at its discretion, may ask for additional securities by way of one 
or more of the following: 
— Government guarantee. 
— Guarantee of a scheduled bank. 
— Personal guarantee of the Directors and collateral security. 
2. New co-operative societies:  
The co-operative societies, which are not in operation for more than three 
years, will normally be assisted through State Govts. However, such co-
operatives in exceptional cases may be considered for direct funding, if in 
addition to the eligibility criteria indicated in para 1 above (as applicable), 
following additional securities are made available: 
(i) Government guarantee or Guarantee of a scheduled bank.

Unsolved issues of Johannesburg Earth Summit 
3159. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister 
of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether even after a document on sustainable development of the Earth 
has been finalised, a number of issues like targets for increase in amount of 
power generated from renewable sources, the insistence of developed 
countries to link the demand for aid with rights recorded and democracy of the 
developing nations, and the latter's demand for cut in subsidies to farmers in 
developed countries, remained unsolved and were subject to controversy; 
(b) if so, the details of the subjects and issues on which controversy 
continued to persist; and 
(c) what steps are being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU):(a) to (c) During the discussions in the World Summit on 
Sustainable Development(WSSD), the question of diversification of energy supply 
by developing advanced and cleaner energy technologies and setting a target 
for renewable energy was extensively debated. The European Union insisted 
on a global target of 2 per cent of renewable energy by the year 2010 from the 
base year 2000. On the basis of their energy resources endowment, Group of 77 
and China and some developed countries were cautious in accepting a firm 
commitment on the share of renewable energy in their overall energy 
requirement. This issue was resolved by including strong and emphatic 
references to increase the share of renewable energy on a global, regional and 
national basis. India succeeded in making developed nations agree on helping the 
developing countries with the necessary financial and technical resources to 
increase the share of renewable energy in a gradual manner. 
During the discussions on agriculture, issues related to the impact of trade 
policies that support micro enterprises, value added agricultural 
108 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
products and re-direction of agricultural subsidies to poverty and hunger 
eradication were discussed. Bracketed text on achieving improvements in 
market access, phasing out of export subsidies and reduction of trade distorting 
practices in agriculture were considered together with other trade related 
issues. However, due to their domestic compulsions, developed countries did 
not agree to lift farm subsidies and thus it did not find place in the agreed texts 
of Political Declaration and Johannesburg Plan of Implementation. 
As against the internationally agreed norm of providing 0.7 per cent of their 
annual GNP as overseas development assistance, developed countries had 
only provided 0.22 per cent of their GNP as ODA to developing countries in 
1997. The Plan of Implementation once again urged the developed countries 
to fulfill this commitment. In their counter arguments developed countries linked 
the aid to good governance at the national level in the developing countries. 
However, India and the other developing countries are of the view that there 
is, in addition to good governance at national level, a need for better coordination 
among various agencies leading to improved international environmental 
governance.

Global warming 
3174. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) what efforts Government are ma king to create an eco-friendly 
environment in the country in light of the statement of the Prime Minister 
at UN Climate Change Conference contradicting the change that 
developing countries generate green house gas emission which are 
unnecessary for their economies; 
- (b) whether Government are mobilizing world opinion so as to motivate 
developed countries to make a greater contribution to check global warming; 
and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a)The steps taken by the Government to create an eco-friendly 
environment in the country and to address greenhouse gas emissions include 
measures relating to energy efficiency, energy conservation, power sector reforms, 
renewable energy programme, fuel switching to cleaner energy, afforestation 
and conservation of forests, efficient utilization of coal, reduction of gas 
flaring, installation of heat recovery systems in oil and power sector, 
st3ndardization of fuel efficient irrigation pump sets and better cultivar 
practices. 
India is a Party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate 
Change which seeks to address climate change in accordance with principles 
of equity, common but differentiated responsibilities and respective 
capabilities. The Convention notes that the largest share of historical and 
current global emissions of greenhouse gases has originated in developed 
countries, that per capita emissions in developing countries are still relatively low 
and that the share of global emissions originating in developing countries will 
grow to meet their social and development needs. 
(b) and (c) India is actively participating in various multilateral forums 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
on climate change. India also acceded to the Kyoto Protocol in August, 2002 
which further affirms India's commitment to strengthening global efforts to 
combat climate change. India also hosted the Eighth Conference of Parties to the 
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change from October 23 to 
November 1, 2002 at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi which is again a reiteration 
of its commitment to the cause of climate change. The Delhi Ministerial 
Declaration, an outcome of the Conference, urges Parties that have not ratified 
the Kyoto Protocol to do so in a timely manner. It also resolves that Annex I 
Parties should further implement their commitments under the Convention, 
including, for Annex- II Parties, those relating to the provision of financial 
resources, technology transfer and capacity-building, and demonstrate that they 
are taking the lead in modifying longer-term trends in anthropogenic 
greenhouse gas emissions, consistent with the ultimate objective of the 
Convention, through the adoption of national policies and corresponding 
measures for the mitigation of climate change.

(b) 60 proposals for granting Deemed to be University status are pending. 
(c) Proposals for Deemed University status are examined in consultation 
with UGC and AICTE. UGC and AICTE have laid down the guidelines for 
considering the proposals for declaring an institution as Deemed to be 
University. These guidelines, inter-alia, provide that an institution should 
generally be:— 
(i) Engaged in teaching programmes and reasearch in chosen fields of 
specialisation which are innovative and very high academic standards at 
the Master's (or equivalent) and/or research levels. It should also have a 
greater interface with society through extra mural, extension and field 
action related programmes. 
(ii) Making in its areas of specialisation, distinct contribution to the 
objectives of the University education system through innovative 
programmes and on being recognised as a university capable of further 
enriching the university system as well as strengthening teaching and 
research in the institution and particularly in its area of specialisation. 
(iii) Competent to undertake application-oriented programmes in emerging 
areas which are relevant and useful to various development sectors and to 
the society in general. 
(iv) Institutions should have the necessary viability and management 
capable of contributing to the university ideals and traditions. 
Ordinarily, institutions affiliated to universities and which are offering only 
conventional degree programmes leading to B.A./B.Com./B.Sc. or 
M.A./M.Com./M.Sc, will not be considered for grant of deemed to be 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
university status. However, such institution which is also offering innovative 
programmes, and which has adequate resources, might be considered for 
recognition as a university. Supplementary assistance for innovation may be 
considered by the UGC only in such exceptional cases. 
Institutions which are imparting routine type of instruction to full-time 
students or offering training programmes for in-service personnel, unless of high 
quality, would, generally, not qualify for recognition. 
In selective cases, outstanding research institutions specialising in Social 
Sciences, Sciences and Technology can be considered for research degree and 
highly specialised programmes at the Master's level. 
In case the institution is offering a degree/diploma, in professional 
subject(s), the academic programme(s) should be recognised by the concerned 
statutory authority e.g. All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), 
Medical Council of India (MCI), Dent al Council of India (DCI), Central 
Council of Homoeopathy (CCH), Indian Nursing Council (INC) etc. before it 
applies for a deemed to be university status under Section 3 of the UGC Act. 
This shall, however, not apply to de-novo institutions in the emerging areas 
with the promise of excellence, not yet fulfilling the prescribed guidelines of 
the UGC whose case will be considered for a provisional status for a Deemed 
to be University. 
(d) UGC has informed that there is a post of President (equivalent to 
Chancellor) in Deemed Universities. Model MOA formulated by UGC for

Strategy for female literacy 
3195. DR. ABRAR AHMED: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what strategies Government have adopted to improve female literacy in the 
country; and 
141 

RAJYA  SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
(b) the progress made, as a result thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan is a National programme for universalisation of elementary 
education through a time bound integrated approach in partnership with 
States. There are special interventions under this programme for the girl child. 
Some of the interventions for education of girl children are: 
• Interventions for Early Childhood Care and Education. 
• School/EGS like alternative facility to be set up within one kilometer of all 
habitations. 
• Up-gradation of EGS to regular schools. 
• Special mainstreaming camps for out-of-school girls/SC/ST children under 
the Alternative and Innovative Education component. 
• Provision of process based community participation with a focus on the 
participation of women and SC/ST. 
• Provision of context specific innovative intervention for girls' education 
and education of SC/ST children upto Rs. 50.00 lakhs in a district in a 
particular year in which the ceiling for each intervention is Rs. 15 lakhs. 
• Mid-day-meal programme. 
• Incentives like uniforms and scholarships to be funded from State Plan 
only. 
• Adequate Teaching Learning Equipment for all Primary and Upper 
Primary schools. 
• At least 50% of the teachers to be appointed have to be women. 
• Special teaching support as per need. 
• Using Community Teachers. 
• Provision of free text books to all girl/SC/ST children at primary and 
upper primary level with an upper ceiling of Rs. 150/- per child. 
• Mahila Samakhya like intervention from the innovation fund is 
operational in 10 States Viz. Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Gujarat, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, 
Jharkhand and Bihar.

National Literacy Mission (NLM) aims at imparting functional literacy to 
non-literates in 15-35 year age group. Major thrust of this programme is on

points i.e. from 39.29% in 1991 to 54.16% in 2001 .The gap in male-female

percentage points in 2001.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) to (c) The Department of Science and 
Technology (DST) organised a Brainstorming session on Monsoon 2002 in 
Bangalore on 28-29 November, 2002 to discuss the causes of failure of this 
year's summer monsoon in the country. In this session, several Scientists from 
India Meteorological Department, Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, 
National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting, New Delhi, Space 
Applications Centre, Ahmedabad, Indian Institute of Technology (NT) New 
Delhi, Centre for Mathematical Modelling and Computer Simulation 
(CMMACS), Cochin University, Andhra University and the Indian Institute of 
Science, Bangalore, participated. 
The monsoon season of 2002 in which the all-India monsoon rainfall was in 
deficit by 19% has turned out to be an intriguing season. None of the methods 
developed for empirical prediction, which have been reasonably successful for over 
a decade could predict this drought. The predictions given in May 2002, on the 
basis of complex atmospheric/climate models by the leading global centres, also 
did not suggest a drought over India. The focus of the meeting was on this 
monsoon season of 2002 with a particular emphasis on July 2002 in which an 
unprecedented deficit of 49% was observed. Observations from India and 
global data were discussed in detail. Empirical predictions for the season as 
well as July were discussed and possible modifications of the models, for 
better predictions of the season and July 2002 were also discussed. 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
The Scientists concluded that predicting extremes such as the severe 
drought remains an extremely challenging problem. However, with further efforts 
in development of empirical methods and more investigations with general 
circulation models, the scientists expect improvement in the skill of prediction 
of rainfall of the season and for the monsoon month of July.To achieve this, a 
multi pronged approach was recommended. More observations over the ocean 
with ships, buoys, floats, etc. are required. Special observational experiments 
such as BOBMEX conducted over the Bay of Bengal in 1999 and ARMEX 
over the Arabian Sea in 2002 are needed on a regular basis. Further research in 
atmospheric models aimed towards developing a unified model which can 
generate robust simulations of the monsoon and its variability is essential. 
More work on ocean models for simulating the conditions over the Indian Ocean 
from the enhanced observational network is necessary. 
Experts from foreign countries did not participate in this meeting.
