GOVERNMENT BILL 
The Competition Bill, 2002 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Thank you, Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity to explain my perceptions in 
this piece of legislation, which was examined and scrutinised by the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee dealing with Home, 
Law, Justice and Company Affairs, at that point of time. Sir, while moving 
the Bill, the hon. Finance Minister pointed out that this Bill was introduced in 
August, 2001, and referred to the Standing Committee. The Standing 
Committee presented its Report after it examined it over a period of one full 
year, in 13 sittings. 
250 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
[THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
Sir, before that also, there were some initiatives taken in respect of 
this Competition Bill. At the initial stage, there were lot of doubts. Naturally, 
our steps were faulty, halting and hesitant. The first announcement in respect 
of the Competition Bill was made by the hon. Finance Minister in his Budget 
Speech of 1999-2000. But, prior to that, the Ministry of Commerce, which is 
the nodal Ministry in respect of World Trade Organisation, after the 
declaration of the Singapore Ministerial Conference, set up an Expert Group, 
under the Chairmanship of Mr. Chakravarthy, to examine the necessity for 
such a Bill in the context of trade and investment. That Expert Group 
examined a large number of issues, including TRIPs, trade and investment, 
trade and competition, anti-dumping and the related matters. After the 
announcement in the Budget, an Expert Group was appointed, under the 
Chairmanship of Mr. Raghvan. After the report of the Experts Group being 
made available, a concept Bill was circulated through the website of the 
Department of Company Affairs, and in the usual process, the consultations 
took place between the various Ministries and the State Governments. 
Ultimately, in this shape, the Bill came. While considering the Bill, there 
were different views. We had a very long discussion; I would not like to go 
into the details of it. But, as it is, in one way, it is a major improvement in our 
corporate governance. Therefore, we shall have to look into it from that 
perspective. The Committee had the privilege of having discussions with not 
only a large number of bodies representing trade, commerce and industry, like 
FICCI, ASSOCHAM, PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, but also a 
large number of professional bodies like the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants, the Institute of Cost Accountants and the lending organisations 
like IDBI and the institutions associated with the stock market like the 
National Stock Exchange and SEBI. After that, the Report was placed, and I 
am happy that the hon. Minister has referred to the fact that, except on three 
areas, the Government has accepted the recommendations of the Committee. 
The Bill which is having 66 clauses deals with certain major aspects, and 
certain conceptual formulations have been made therein. They require not only 
the attention of the Government but also of all those who are concerned with 
it. 
The very fundamental question arose whether the MRTP Act which 
was passed by both Houses of Parliament in 1969 could do this job; and, 
whether, by making certain appropriate amendments in the MRTP Act, the 
objective of advocating competition, preventing restrictive trade practices, 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
and encouraging competition could have been possible or not. It was found 
that, with the changing scenario, and, specially, with the opening up of the 
economy, with the growing globalisation, the institutional arrangements and 
the legal framework which were available in a, more or less, controlled 
economy would not be adequate to reflect the situation prevailing right now. 
For example, Madam, in the early eighties, only 40 countries of the world had 
the competition law. Even a country like United Kingdom did not have the 
competition law till 1996, and, today, more than one hundred countries have 
already established the competition law. Trade and competition is going to be 
a debatable subject in the series of negotiations, which are coming, related to 
the WTO. Therefore, it was considered necessary to have an appropriate legal 
framework to encourage competition and also to make a departure from the 
practices which we used to have. If we look at the entire thrust of the MRTP 
Act, it was on that side, and my colleague, Dr. Singh, as Finance Minister, had 
to do away with these aspects of the MRTP Act even before we 
conceptualised about the introduction of the Competition Bill. In the mid 
eighties, the ceiling which was fixed for the monopoly houses was expanded 
and later on removed. Today, competition is going to be the crux of not only 
in the manufacturing sector but also in many other areas. Therefore, there is a 
need for competition advocacy. One of the major objectives of this Bill, for 
which a legal framework is being provided, is to protect the consumers. There 
would be extreme difficulties, if somebody abuses the dominance. The new 
concept that has been brought in this Bill is that dominance as such is not bad, 
but abuse of dominance is bad. To prevent the abuse of dominance an 
institutional arrangement, in the form of the Competition Commission of 
India, is being established. As regards the procedure of appointment of

255 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
the MRTP regime. The MRTP law was legislated in 1969 when the regime 
was more regulated. The MRTP Act was enacted to deal with restrictive and 
unfair trade practices. As Shri Pranab Mukherjee has pointed out, it was 
enacted on the presumption that the size of a corporation was something 
which was to be eminently discouraged. When the law was originally enacted, 
in fact, the size of the business world was almost regarded as an evil. But this 
became somewhat irrelevant to the present times. We need our corporations 
today to compete globally. We need them to be very large in size. We also 
need them to benefit from the economies of scale. But, at the same time, we 
must also take care that no abuse of that takes place. The second reason why 
the MRTP Act has lost its relevance is, as it was pointed out, there are areas

moving away from the MRTP Commission and what remains now is a 
restrictive trade practice. The MRTP Act has 17 trade practices which are 
referred to, per se as restrictive trade practices. In a market regulated 
economy, perhaps, a very large number of them may not even be regarded as 
restrictive trade practices in the present context. So the Competition Bill has 
been brought keeping this thing in mind. The Competition Bill has three basic 
components. The underlying intention of each of the three components is that 
in a free market economy or a regulated economy, when aberrations start from 
the market itself, should the economy and the Government and the system be 
helpless in dealing with those aberrations? You give them freedom, but you 
expect a certain amount of fairness along with that freedom. And, that fairness 
will be ensured by putting a regulatory mechanism and the rules in place 
which every corporation has to follow. The first component, therefore, which 
is dealt with under clause 3 of this Bill is the anti-competitive practices. There 
is a complete prohibition that no corporation, no company, shall indulge in 
any form of anti-competitive practices. I may mention here that those 17 
restrictive trade practices under the MRTP Act have been reduced, on a 
presumption, to four anticompetitive practices. Now, these are four- anti-
competitive practices which are eminently presumed to be per se anti-
competitive. One instance is large companies which control the market share, 
starting regulating the sale price. The object of competition is, when 
competition increases, quality will improve, quantums will improve, prices 
will come down and the consumer will benefit. The essence of this law is that 
the consumer interest is to be protected.   It is a macro law unlike the 
Consumer Protection Act, which is a 
256 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
micro law to redress the grievances of the consumer, which protects through 
the market economy, the interest of the consumer. But, if ail of them gang up, 
all of them form a cartel, and then the says, "None of us will sell below this 
price" -- we had last year instances of cement companies in this country doing 
it -- in such a case, will the system be helpless or will there be a forum like 
Competition Commission which will have the jurisdiction to pass appropriate 
orders to crack and break a cartel of this kind? Another anti-competitive 
practice, besides cartelisation in terms of prices, is also to limit the supply. 
We find in the international oil arena, at times, the oil supplies are restricted 
and the result of it is that prices go up. So, if you restrict supplies, consumer 
interest is adversely affected. The third is, you can divide markets to eliminate 
competition. You can say somebody will sell only in the East and somebody 
else will sell only in the West, so that in the respective geographical markets, 
competition is eliminated. Now, this is per se an anti-competitive practice. 
The other instance of anti-corrupt practice, which is given, is collusive 
bidding or bid-rigging in matters of c ontracts. Now, these are four practices, 
which are per se regarded as anti-competitive; they are prohibited, they will 
be penalised, but there can be other market practices also in addition to these 
four, which, by rule of reason, can be anti-competitive. That is the essence of 
the first part of this law and I feel that this is one aspect, which requires to be 
put in force at the earliest. The second component of this Bill relates to size. 
But, unlike the MRTP Act, it doesn't consider size per se as evil Market

pockets, which can sell below the cost price. By doing so, it can eliminate 
competition and once competition is eliminated, it can create a situation 
where it can exploit the market. These are two aspects of this Bill which are

Commission, which, I do not think, there is any dispute about. But, one area

economies, the principle that they have followed is that if the effect of a 
merger or an amalgamation is to have an appreciable adverse effect on 
competition, that 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
is to say, if there are four large scooter manufacturers in India and they decide

Disinvestment of the Paradeep Phosphates Limited 
THE MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND MINISTER 
OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATIONS TECHNOLOGY (SHRI 
PRAMOD MAHAJAN): Madam, on 19 th December, hon. Mr. Kapil Sibal 
raised some issues regarding the Paradeep Phosphates Limited and the hon. 
Chairman directed that somebody from the Government should get the 
information and share it with the House. So, I got the information from the 
Disinvestment Ministry and the Disinvestment Minister, who is in Sri Lanka 
at this point of time. As they have given the information, I will read out the 
information for the benefit of the House: 
"PPL was referred to the Disinvestment Commission. Based on the 
recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission, the Government 
decided to disinvest 74 per cent of its equity through strategic sale. The 
financial bids for 74 per cent equity of the company were invited on the basis 
of the last Balance Sheet of PPL, that is, for 2000-2001 and the process of 
strategic sale was concluded on 28 th February, 2002, with the signing of the 
transaction agreements among the Government, the Company and the 
strategic partner, namely, M/s. Zuari Maroc Phosphates Private Limited. The 
consideration paid by the strategic partner for the equity disinvested was Rs. 
151.70 crores. 
Prior to disinvestment, 100 per cent of the equity of PPL was held by 
the Government of India and the company was unlisted. The Company had 
been incurring severe losses over the years and in spite of several financial 
restructurings being undertaken by the Government, on 31 * March, 2001, its 
net worth was Rs. 1.15 crores and accumulated losses amounted to Rs.431.50 
crores. At the time of disinvestment, Government was aware that PPL had 
continued to incur losses during 2001-02 and that its net worth would further 
deteriorate. The Government also finalized the strategic sale in the knowledge 
that such sale was the only viable alternative to reduce the losses of the 
Government. 
The transaction agreements relating to the disinvestment in most 
unlisted companies provide for the post-closure adjustments. Such provisions 
exist in the agreements relating to disinvestment in Bharat Aluminium 
Company Limited, Modern Food Industries (India) Limited, HTL Limited 
and in hotels of India Tourism Development Corporation and Hotel 
Corporation  of  India  Limited.     In  the  case  of PPL also,  like  in  other 
286 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
companies, there is a provision for the post-closure adjustments. The 
transaction agreements were circulated to all the qualified bidders (namely, 
M/s Rastriya Chemicals and Fertilizers Limited, M/s Tata Chemicals 
Limited, M/s Zuari and M/s Oswal Chemicals and Fertilizers Limited) before 
inviting financial bids, and the bidders had full knowledge of eligibility for 
post-closure adjustment. 
PPL continued to remain under Government management till 28 th 
February, 2002. Given the gap between the date of the last Balance Sheet 
provided to the bidder and the closing date of the transaction, it was 
recognized that the asset/liability position of the company would undergo a 
change and therefore, a post-closing audit of the accounts of the company 
would become necessary to assess and finally determine the actual 
improvement/deterioration in the assets/liabilities position during the 
intervening period. The transaction agreements, therefore, provided that if the 
closing date net asset amount was greater than that of the last Balance Sheet 
Net Asset Amount, M/s Zuari Maroc Phosphates Private Limited was 
obligated to pay the Government the differences whereas if the closing date 
net asset amount were lesser than that of the last balance sheet net asset 
amount, the Government was under obligation to pay the difference. 
The financial condition of some of the Central/State public sector 
companies and undertakings are so bad that the Government has and had to 
take over or restructure thousands of crores of rupees of liabilities before or 
during the disinvestment process. In all such cases, the likelihood of financial 
restructuring or the possibility of post-closure adjustment has been clearly 
divulged before calling financial bids. 
It is well known that the state of accounts in some public sector 
undertakings, particularly loss-making, leave much to be desired. It is inter 
alia on account of this reason that bidders insist on post-closure adjustment 
provision and without such provision, no bids are likely to be received.

firm to prepare the closing date net assets amount would be jointly selected 
by the seller and the buyer and such selected auditor has to prepare the 
closing date statement in accordance with the existing accounting principles 
and norms adopted by the company while preparing the last balance sheet. It 
is under this provision that M/s. Price Water House has been appointed to 
prepare closing date net assets amount statement and has submitted its

VALEDICTORY REMARKS 
(MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, the month-long Winter Session 
is now coming to an end. I recall, on this date, last month, how warmly and 
generously you had welcomed me as a part of you, and assured me of your 
fullest cooperation. Today, I must acknowledge that the understanding shown 
and the cooperation and support extended by all of you, has been much 
beyond anyone's expectations. My sincere and grateful thanks for the same. I 
crave for your continued goodwill and indulgence in future as well. 
I had made a solemn promise of equal and respectful treatment to all 
and had assured of my sincere efforts to make the functioning of this House 
more productive and more effective. I had also suggested that, henceforth, we 
should evaluate, at the end of every Session, as to how relevant and fruitful 
the proceedings have been, from the viewpoint of contribution towards 
improving governance and public welfare. 
Hon. Members, I am happy to say that thanks to your invaluable 
support, we certainly have achieved considerable and significant success. 
With sober and dignified conduct of the proceedings, purposeful as well as 
focussed discussion and debate on important public issues, this august House 
has-been successful in setting up new standards and be a good role model for 
other elected bodies. 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2002] 
In the total sittings of 23 days, the House has set a record of 
uninterrupted Question Hour on each day; the average number of questions 
taken up in a day has shown a marked increase, which resulted in larger 
number of Members getting the opportunity to participate. In the area of 
Legislative Business, in all, 35 Bills were passed, covering some very 
important subjects, such as consumer welfare, conservation of biodiversity, 
electoral reforms, development of the North-East, welfare of SCs and STs, 
and financial sector reforms. This would help in improving the policy 
framework for programmes of development and better governance in our 
country. 
It is also very satisfying that during this Session, the House had 
purposeful and very productive discussions in the form of Short Duration 
Discussion, on important issues, such as the drought situation in various parts 
of the country, political developments in Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh, 
Disinvestment of PSUs, Mid-Year Review of the Economy, and international 
development concerning West Asia. Constructive and serious discussion on 
such issues surely goes a long way in focussing attention for appropriate and 
suitable action by the concerned authorities. 
Hon. Members also took up various issues of urgent public 
importance through Calling-Attention as well as Special Mentions. In this 
Session, five Calling-Attentions were taken up and discussed. The device of 
Special Mentions is a very useful means of raising issues of public 
importance; this is very evident from the fact that more than 130 Special 
Mentions were made in this Session. 
Hon. Members, this was my first Session. It has been a very rich, 
learning, experience. Frankly, in the beginning, I was quite diffident; many 
persons told me how difficult it was going to be to run the House. But, on the 
strength of your cooperation, support and goodwill, I have had no difficulty 
whatsoever. The credit for whatever success we have been able to achieve 
towards making our functioning more effective and productive is entirely 
yours. We, together, should endeavour for even greater success, bigger 
achievements and better participation in future. 
On behalf of the hon. Deputy Chairperson, Members of the Panel of 
Vice-Chairman, and my own behalf, I thank the Leader of the House, the 
Leader of the Opposition, leaders of various political parties and groups, and 
all the hon. Members, for their kind cooperation in conducting the 
proceedings of the House. 
Before we adjourn, may I extend to you all the Season's Greetings 
294 

[20 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
and my very good wishes for a very happy and prosperous New Year?

THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN 
SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I join all my colleagues in paying our warm 
tributes to the leadership that you provided to our House in our deliberations. 
We have accomplished a great deal by way of legislation, and for this, you, 
the Deputy Chairman.the hon. Minister of Parliamentary Affairs and the hon. 
the Leader of the House deserve sincere thanks. We have always taken a view 
that our role is that of a constructive Opposition, and it is in that spirit we 
have approached our task. Sir, as you have just now mentioned, apart from 
legislation, a large number of issues have been discussed in this House. We 
draw comfort from some progress being made in several burning issues of 
public importance.   But we feel that a lot more needs to be done. 
We discussed the external situation with regard to-the West Asian 
region. The situation in areas around Iraq continues to be a cause of concern. 
It is our hope and prayer that the solution to the problems that have arisen will 
be found through peaceful means. And, it is to that objective we expect the 
Government of India also to pledge itself. Sir, we are disappointed with 
certain aspects of foreign policy. The SAARC faces an uncertain future. 
Whatever our bilateral concerns with Pakistan may be, we should never flinch 
from making efforts to strengthen the SAARC. All over the world, people are 
moving towards closer and closer regional integration. It is the misfortune of 
South Asia that regional cooperation has not been taken up. I recognise the 
difficulties that arise because of our bilateral relations with Pakistan. But that 
should not be the reason to forget the basic objectives of the SAARC. The 
future of this Sub-continent and South Asia lies in cooperation and not in 
confrontation. 
Sir, in the same way, we have seen in recent months the onslaught of 
terrorism, its domestic implications and its international implications. We are 
all one in the sense that we all agree that our country must have an effective 
anti-terrorism strategy. But I sincerely hope, in the name of such a strategy we 
will not communalise the situation in our country. 
Sir, we have had a historic election in Jammu & Kashmir. I had 
hoped that we would find some way of having a discussion on the 
implications of this peaceful, free and fair election that took place.   We take 
295

pride in the fact that despite tremendous difficulties, we were able to conduct 
a free and fair poll in Jammu & Kashmir. Sir, the Government that has come 
into being, I think, needs the unanimous support of all sections of this House 
to tackle the most difficult problems that it faces - the problem of ending the 
alienation of a certain section of the youth in Jammu and Kashmir, and 
ensuring that the pace of development is accelerated. I submit even at this late 
hour to the Government that they should set up a high powered Ministerial 
group to look into the special proble ms that Jammu & Kashmir faces in 
meeting the challenges that lie ahead. 
Sir, we have had a very fruitful discussion on natural calamities, 
drought in one part of the country and floods in another. But having listened 
to the debate, I have a strong feeling that the time has come to take a holistic 
view of our approach to tackle the problem of natural calamities. In many 
ways, when it comes to drought, the Famine Code of 1880 still remains the 
Bible. Times have changed, and I do feel that the Government should take a 
fresh look at the basic approach to tackling the problems of natural calamities 
-- who should get benefit, for how long -- so that these unnatural situations 
that prevail, of acute destitution, become a thing of the past. 
We had a very useful discussion on the current economic situation. 
But, at the end of all this, we are not sure about the means that the 
Government proposes to adopt to move towards the targeted growth rate 
which has been mentioned in the draft document of the Tenth Five-Year Plan. 
These are some of the concerns that we have. But, in conclusion, 
once again, I would like to thank you, on my behalf and on my party's behalf, 
for the excellent quality of leadership that you have provided to all of us. It is 
our great asset to have you as our Chairman. I also take this opportunity to 
thank the hon. Leader of the House, the hon. Minister of Parliamentary 
Affairs, the hon. Deputy Chairman and the staff of the Rajya Sabha 
Secretariat who have worked so hard to make this Session a highly 
satisfactory experience for all of us.  Thank you.

Commencing on the   17th  February, 2003/28 Magha, 1924 (Saka) 

[17 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
RAJYA SABHA 
Monday, the 17th  February, 2003/23 Magha, 1 924 (Saka) 
The House met at two  of the clock, 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair.

PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS LAID ON THE TABLE 
SECRETARY-GENERAL: Sir. I beg to lay on the Table of the 
House a copy of the President's Address to both the Houses of Parliament 
assembled together on 17th  February. 2003. 
[Text of the Address delivered by the President {Dr. A.P.J. Abdul 
Kalam) ] : 
Honourable Members, 
I extend a warm welcome to you at this first session of Parliament in 
2003. This is my first Address to Parliament at the start of the Budget 
Session. 
Let me first welcome the newly elected Members of the Rajya 
Sabha, as also of the Lok Sabha. I congratulate the people of Jammu and 
Kashmir who, in the October elections to the State Assembly, replied to the 
threat of the bullet with the power of the ballot. The entire Nation is grateful 
to our Armed Forces, Paramilitary Fo rces, and Police Forces for their 
dedicated service under extremely trying conditions. We pay our homage to 
those who became martyrs in the call of their duty. 
Today I would like all of you to join me in paying tribute to Kalpana 
Chawla and her six fellow astronauts, who died in the tragic break-up of 
Space Shuttle Columbia minutes before its touchdown on February i. The 
remarkable journey of courage and determination that made this Indian 
woman, hailing from a small town in Haryana, a Citizen of the Milky Way 
will remain a source of pride for all Bharatvasis and Bharatvanshis, It will 
also inspire young Indians, especially women, to dream big and to work hard 
to realize their dreams, i commend ISRO's gesture in naming the METSAT 
series of satellites after Kalpana Chawla. 
 
1

RAJYA SABHA       [17 February, 2003] 
This is the first session of Parliament after the National Development 
Council adopted the Tenth FIve-Year Plan. The Plan aims at accomplishing 
faster economic growth with a stronger thrust on employment generation and 
equity. It has set the target of 8 per cent annua! average GDP growth rate 
during the Plan period, with a companion target of 5 crore additional 
employment ^d self-em.ployment opportunities. The Plan convincingly 
explains why these ambitious goals are achievable. It has distinguished itself 
from the previous Plans by underscoring that it is not merely a Resources 
Plan, but a Reforms Plan. It has deepened the domain of economic reforms 
by, especially, providing reforms-linked incentives to State Governments. It 
has also broadened the agenda of reforms by showing the categorical 
imperative to remove numerous non-financial barriers to faster development 
through reforms in civil service, judiciary, education, and above all, in 
governance at all levels - at the Centre, States, and Panchayati Raj 
Institutions. I would especially like to draw the attention of the Union and 
State Governments to the detailed list, contained in the Plan document, of the 
legislative and administrative initiatives needed to translate the Tenth Plan's 
goals and targets into reality. 
The Tenth Plan is important for yet another reason. No nation attains 
greatness without an energizing vision guiding it. The Prime Minister, in his 
Independence Day address last year, has called upon the people to strive 
towards the goal of transforming India into a Developed Nation by 2020. This 
vision captures our people's heightened self-confidence, rooted in India's 
impressive achievements in many fields. It also reflects the increased 
expectations of our people at the beginning of the new century, that India no 
longer be categorized as a developing, much less, a poor country. Nearly 260 
million people, who are below the poverty line, want to join the mainstream of 
development. Our people are impatient to achieve lOO per cent literacy, health 
for all, shelter for all, prosperity through knowledge-driven productivity, and a 
better quality of life - all of these enriched with our value system. Hence, it is 
time India launched a new vision, which I would call "Vision - 2020". I would 
like Parliament, which is celebrating its Golden ' Jubilee, to discuss this 
subject. I also call upon the Union and State governments to evolve an action 
plan for making the Tenth Plan a People's Plan and Development a People's 
Movement. To achieve this, they should concentrate on two mantras: Effective 
Imptementation with  People's Participation; and Effective Communication for 
People's Participation. 
 
2

[17 February. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
A key element of "Vision 2020" would be "Providing Urban 
amenities in Rural Areas (PURA)'. More than two-thirds of India's population 
lives in rural areas. We need to give a new thrust to their all-round 
development through a mega mission for their empowerment. This is best 
achieved through provision of four critical connectivities: Physical 
Connectivity by providing good roads, transport services and quality power; 
Electronic Connectivity by providing reliable communication networks; 
Knowledge Connectivity by establishing more professional institutions and 
vocational training centres, schools with high quality infrastructure, teachers 
who are devoted to teaching, production centres for rural artisans, primary 
health centres, recreation centres, etc; and Market Connectivity that will help

and minorities has been the constant endeavour of my Government. One of the 
key strategies for ensuring this Is through economic justice and employment-
oriented educational assistance. In the current year over 18 lakh SCs, 5 lakh 
STs and 6 lakh backward class students have been awarded scholarships, Two 
new merit-based scholarships after loth standard have been introduced this 
year - one in the name of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar and the other for 
physically challenged students. The various concerned Finance and 
Development Corporations have a challenging role to play to live up to their 
mandate. 
To give a further thrust to the v^relfare and development of 
Scheduled Tribes, a Scheduled Area and Scheduled Tribes Commission has 
been set up. The last such Commission was set up in i960. Similarly, after 
fifty years, a summary revision of Scheduled Tribes' list has been done under 
Article 342 of the Constitution, involving inclusion or excfusion of 142 
communities. To give focused attention to the needs of Scheduled Tribes, it 
17 

RAJYA SABHA       [17 February, 2003] 
is   proposed   to   set   up   a  separate   National   Commission  for  STs  by 
bifurcating the National Commission for SCs and STs. 
The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports has finalized a new draft 
National Youth Policy. A National Youth Commission has been set up. Indian 
sportspersons deserve commendation on their spectacular performance in the 
17th Commonwealth Games and I4th Asian Games. The decision to host the 
first ever Afro-Asian Games later this year will further promote sports in the 
country. I call upon our promising spor tspersons and sports organizations to 
start preparing in full swing for the Olympics next year. Honourable 
Members, let us send our best wishes to the Indian cricket team playing in the 
World Cup tournament in South Africa. 
The Government's commitment to electoral reforms is seen in the 
concrete legislative action undertaken last year. It showed that Parliament is 
responsive to people's concerns over criminalisation of politics. Further, the 
Representation of the People (Amendment) Bill, 2001 seeking to provide for 
open ballot system in respect of elections to Rajya Sabha for checking 
reported prevalence of money power in Rajya Sabha elections, and the 
Election and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2002 providing election 
funding to political parties to check con-uption and money power in elections, 
are pending before Parliament. 
Judicial delays have been a cause for serious concern, To remedy 
this situation, nearly Rs. 500 crore have been allocated as special project and 
upgradation grant for judicial administration. This is the largest investment 
ever made for this purpose. Fast Track Courts in some States have improved 
the conviction rate. A concerted drive has been launched to fill about 2,000 
vacant posts of Judges and Magistrates in District and Subordinate Courts. 
The year gone by has seen a bouquet of initiatives to revive the glory 
of Indian culture. The much-needed synergy between Culture and Tourism has 
been brought to the fore by promoting a new concept of 'developing at least 
one Culture-cum-Tourlst hub in each State. A number of monuments have 
been taken up for integrated conservation and development. All-round 
infrastructure development and public amenities around these complexes have 
been taken up in a big way. Kurukshetra, Red Fort, Ajanta, Eliora, Hampi, 
Humayun's Tomb, etc. are some of the 
18 

[17 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
examples. It is proposed to revive cultural tourism along the routes of the 
great Yatras of Adi Shankaracharya, Swami Vivekananda, and Mahatma 
Gandhi. Work is being undertaken to develop complexes along the route of 
the legendary river Saraswati. Many schemes have been taken up during 
commemoration of 2,600 years of the Janm Kalyanak of Bhagwan Mahavir. 
The Mahabharata Festival at Kurukshetra will now be held every year. Much 
of the ancient wisdom of India Is stored in a large number of manuscripts 
available with institutions and Individuals all across the country. A National 
Mission for Manuscripts has been recently launched wdh the aim of 
surveying, cataloguing, preserving and collecting these invaluable 
manuscripts in a National Manuscripts Library. 
My Government will continue its vigorous efforts to use India's 
Foreign Policy to promote and safeguard our critical national interests. 
Drawing on the strength of our civilizational and historical ties with countries 
across the globe, we will forge ahead towards broad-basing our political links, 
expanding our network of economic cooperation, strengthening strategic 
inter-linkages, and collaborating on cutting-edge technologies. 
India has always striven for peaceful, friendly, and cooperative 
relations vwth all its neighbours. Unfortunately, Pakistan has consistently 
responded to our efforts with hatred and violence, sponsoring and actively 
supporting a sustained campaign of cross-border terrorism. Recent revelations 
have shown how every civilized diplomatic norm is being flouted by the use 
of its diplomatic mission in Delhi to arrange financing for terrorist groups in 
the country. We have had to take measures against the concerned diplomats, 
but have also reiterated that we would be willing to retain the level of our 
diplomatic representations by accepting replacements of the expelled officials. 
Our position remains unchanged that we are willing to resume bilateral 
dialogue with Pakistan, as soon as cross-border terrorism ends. 
India's commitment to SAARC, as an engine for economic 
integration and equitable development in the region, remains undiluted. We 
have constantly pushed for progress on substantive aspects of the economic 
agenda outlined in the Kathmandu- Declaration, We have repeatedly declared 
our willingness to attend the next SAARC Summit if meaningful progress is 
achieved on these issues.

India will continue to intensify its multi-faceted cooperation with 
Bhutan. Historical, cultural, and ethnic affinities have shaped our relations 
with Bangladesh and Myanmar. We are also implementing developmental 
projects with Indian assistance in Myanmar. With Bangladesh, we are also 
engaged in a dialogue on some important political and security issues that 
have arisen in our interactions. The visit of the Prime Minister to Maldives in 
September last year further enhanced our cordial relationship with that 
country. 
Nepal is passing through a difficult phase of political changes and 
Maoist insurgency. We believe that multiparty democracy and constitutional 
monarchy are two essential pillars for stability, security, and development in 
Nepal. We hope that the current problems will be resolved within this 
framework, in a peaceful and consensual atmosphere. We have maintained an 
intensive political dialogue and fruitful economic cooperation with Sri Lanka. 
We continue to support efforts towards a solution of political problems in that 
country In a manner that preserves its territorial integrity and meets the 
aspirations of all segments of its population. 
The people of India and Afghanistan have a legacy of close and 
historic ties of friendship and cooperation. We welcome the expansion and 
consolidation of the authority of the Transitional Administration and fully 
support the Government of Afghanistan. We look fonward to receiving the 
President of Afghanistan on a State visit to India in the very near future. India 
will continue to extend extensive humanitarian, financial, and project 
assistance for Afghanistan's reconstruction. 
The close ties of friendship between India and Iran were put on a 
stronger footing, when we hosted the President of the Islamic Republic of Iran 
as the Chief Guest at our Republic Day Parade this year. We want to expand, 
consolidate, and diversify our ties with Iran, which have a strategic dimension 
in the areas of energy and transit. 
India's interactions with China have grown and diversified. Trade 
and economic cooperation are expanding rapidly. Efforts to build trust and 
understanding in other areas continue. The Prime Minister has been invited to 
visit China this year and has accepted the invitation. We continue to 
strengthen our bilateral relationship with Japan, pursuing the shared objective  
of building  a Global  Partnership.   India's  cooperation  with  the

Republic of Korea continues to expand. We continue to monitor 
developments in the Korean Peninsula. Reports that the Democratic People's 
Republic of Korea resumed its nuclear weapon programme with the help of 
technology from Pakistan arouse serious concern, t>oth about the security 
implications and about the double standards with which much of the world 
has handled the question of treaty obligations as well as proliferation issues. 
India's traditionally warm relations with South East Asia have been 
reflected in our recent bilateral interactions, including the Prime Minister's 
visits to Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand. Our engagement with the region 
reached a qualitatively higher platform, when our interface with ASEAN was 
raised to the Summit level in November 2002. We are making good progress 
on the economic initiatives outlined at the India-ASEAN Summit in Phnom 
Penh. 
India's deep-rooted relations with Central Asia have been enhanced 
by an identity of views on recent political and economic developments. India 
and the countries of Central Asia also have a shared determination to tackle 
the negative focus of terrorism, extremism, and drug trafficking, which stalk 
our common neighbourhood. 
The Gulf region is of great importance to India. The region is a 
major source of India's energy needs and a major economic partner in trade 
and investment. Over 3.5 million Indians are engaged in the economic 
development of the Gulf countries. These multi-dimensional ties have been 
further strengthened and diversified through sustained interaction. 
We share the concern of the entire world on the unhappy situation 
relating to Iraq. We have deep interest in peace, stability, and security in that 
region. We hope that the wisdom of the international community, expressed 
through the UN Security Council, will result in a peaceful resolution of this 
matter in a manner, which would benefit humanity. 
My   Government   attaches   great   importance   to   the   strategic 
partnership between India and the Russian Federation, which is enriched by 
regular political consultations, multi-faceted economic cooperation and 
intensive defence collaboration.  During  President Vladimir Putin's visit to

Underatanding on Cooperation in Fighting against Terrorism. 
India's engagement with countries in Europe continues to be broad-
based and intensive, Regular exchanges of views on regional and international 
developments have promoted a better appreciation in these countries of our 
legitimate concerns and helped to re-vitalize our bilateral relationships. The 
India-EU Summit in Copenhagen strengthened our institutional dialogue with 
the European Union, which we will take forward at the next Summit meeting 
in India later this year. 
India and the USA continue to forge a new relationship. There is a 
mutual conviction between the two countries that their bilateral relationship 
must undergo a qualitative transformation in order to respond to the 
increasingly complex challenges to the international security and strategic 
architecture. The two countries are also engaged in building closer bilateral 
consultations on multilatferat social and economic issues of mutual concern. 
Africa continues to occupy a special place in our diplomatic 
interactions. This continent, which constitutes the largest group of countries in 
the United Nations, is also, increasingly, becoming an important economic 
partner for India. 
Our bilateral relations wfth Latin America and Caribbean have 
grown considerably. The "Focus LAC programme pursued since 1997 has 
resulted in increasing attention being paid to the region by the Indian public 
and private sector. 
The Government's consistent efforts to nurture a close relationship 
with the overseas Indian community were highlighted by the celebrations of 
the first Pravasi Bharatiya Conference In January. On this occasion, we 
honoured ten eminent persons of Indian origin whose achievements in their 
countries of adoption and domicile have done our country proud. The 
Government has also decided to grant dual citizenship for persons of Indian 
origin living in certain countries. Th e necessary legislation for this will be 
introduced in this session.

Honourable Members, it is indeed heartening that the Winter 
Session of Parliament did exceptionally well in conducting its legislative 
business. During that session, both Houses passed as many as 42 Bills and I 
have accorded assent to all of them. The Government was able to bring 
forward several legislations last year, out of which 93 Bills have been passed, 
which also include important constitutional amendments. This Is the highest 
number of enactment of legislations enacted in a single year during the last 25 
years and the third highest since 1947. Apart from the fiscal agenda relating

one.

OBITUARY REFERENCES 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, 1 have to refer with 
profound sorrow to the. passing away of Shri Devendra Prasad Singh, 
Shrimati Annapurna Devi Thimmal Reddy, Dr. Harbans Rai Bachchan and 
Shri Kamal Nath Jha, fonner Members of this House. 
Shri Devendra Prasad Singh passed away on the 29"^ 
September, 2002 at the age of 90 years. Born at Gaziapur. District Sahabad, 
Bihar in June, 1913, Shri Singh had his education at Banaras Hindu 
University and Patna' Law College. 
An agriculturist and advocate by profession, Shri Singh was the 
founder member of the Congress Socialist Party. He was member of the 
Executive Committee of Bihar Prajatantrik Socialist Party in the years 1957 
and 1956. He was associated with various social and welfare organisations. 
Shri Singh represented the State of Bihar in this House from April, 
1958 to April, 1964. 
In the passing away of Shri Devendra Prasad Singh, the country has 
lost a noted social worker. 
Shrimati Annapurna Devi Thimmal Reddy passed away on the 14"" 
November, 2002 at the age of 88 years. Bom at Dodleru, District Guntur, 
Andhra Pradesh in the year 1914, Shrimati Annapurna Devi had her 
education at Saradaniketanam. Guntur. 
A scholar of Sanskrit and an agriculturist by vocation, Shrimati 
Annapurna Devi actively participated during 1937 in the movement for 
establishment of a responsible Governmant in Mysore State. She was 
associated with various social and welfare institutions. She was also a Gold 
Medalist in Carnatic Music, both vocal and instrumental. 
Shrimati Annapurna Devi represented the State of Karnataka 
(erstwhile Mysore State) in this Hous e for two consecutive terms from April, 
1958 to April, 1964 and again from April, 1964 to April, 1970. 
In the passing away of Shrimati Annapurna Devi the country has 
lost a noted social worker. 
Dr. Harbans Rai Bachchan passed away on the is''' January, 2003, at 
the age of 96 years, after a prolonged illness.   Born at

RAJYA SABHA       [1 7 February, 2003] 
Allahabad in November, i907, Dr, Bachchan had his education at Allahabad 
University, Banaras Hindu University and St. Catherines College, Cambridge 
University. 
A prolific Vi/riter and a renowned poet, Dr. Bachchan started his 
career as a Lecturer in English in the Allahabad University in I94i. He taught 
there till 1952 and thereafter he joined the Cambridge University as a 
Research Scholar. In 1954-55, he again taught at the Allahabad University. 
He had a short stint as Producer in the All India Radio, Allahabad from 
October to December, 1955. Dr. Bachchan joined Ministry of External Affairs 
as Officer on Special Duty In the December, 1955 and worked there till 
March, 1966. During his tenure in the Ministry, Dr. Bachchan helped in the 
development of Hindi as the official language. 
In a literary career spanning over more than 50 years, Dr. Bachchan 
achieved fame and recognition in the literary world at a young age of 28 
years, when in the year 1935 he recited Madhushala in front of a huge 
audience enthralling the listeners with the charm like that of Omar Khayyam. 
His autobiography Kya Bhoolun Kya Yaad Karoon is regarded a literary 
masterpiece till date. Apart from these, he had several publications to his 
credit. 
A recipient of Padma Bhusan, Dr. Bachchan won many laurels for his 
contributions to Hindi Literature, The Soviet Land Nehru Award was conferred 
on him for his book Chaunsat Roosi Kavitayen. He won Sahitya Akademi 
Award for his book Do Chattanen. The Hindi Sahitya Sammelan also 
honoured him with the Honorary Degree of Sahitya Vachaspati. He was aiso a 
recipient of Saraswati Samman and Afro-Asian Writers Conference Lotus 
Prize. 
In recognition to his contribution to the world of literature 
particularly Hindi language, he was nominated by the President to the Rajya 
Sabha In April, 1966. 
In the passing away of Dr. Bachchan, the country has lost an 
eminent personality and the literary world, a poetic soul. 
Shri Kamal Nath Jha passed away on the 11'^ February, 2003 at the 
age of 80 years. Born at village Bangian, District Saharsa, Bihar in August, 
1923, Shri Jha had his education at T.N.J, College, Bhagalpur, Bihar.

right from his college days and was imprisoned on several occasions. He gave 
up studies to join the freedom movement in 1942 and organized underground 
armed resistance force known as Azad Dasta in Purnea District and Vi'as 
arrested as secuhty prisoner under DIR in 1944. Shri Jha also organized and 
conducted the Crop Shares Movement. 
Shri Kamal Nath Jha had a long political career, vt/hich started with 
the membership of Bihar Legislative Assembly from 1962 to 1967- He 
represented the State of Bihar in this House from March, 1973 to April, 1974 
and again from April, 1974 to January, i980. Shri Jha was also a Member of 
the 7'" Lok Sabha, 
In the passing away of Shri Kamal Nath Jha, the country has lost a 
veteran freedom fighter and a noted parliamentarian. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Devendra Prasad Singh, 
Shrimati Annapurna Devi Thimmal Reddy, Dr. Harbans Rai Bachchan and 
Shri Kamal Nath Jha.

Statement 
(a) For the year 2002-2003, per capita allocation for distribution under Public

 (Litres/annum)

Assam 12.6

*2. SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: †  
   SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Unit Trust of India (UTI) has been split into two parts 
namely UTI-I and UTI-II; 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by  Shri V.V.

5 

RAJYA  SABHA [18 February, 2003] 
(b) if so, the details and functions of each of them; and 
(c) what is the purpose of splitting it into two parts? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Under the provisions of the Unit Trust of India (Transfer of 
Undertaking and Repeal) Act, 2002, the erstwhile Unit Trust of India has 
been bifurcated, with effect from 1 st February, 2003, into (a) the "specified 
undertaking" viz. UTI-I, comprising of schemes mentioned in Schedule—I 
of the above Act and managed by Government appointed Administrator, 
and (b) the "specified company" viz. UTI-II, comprising of NAV based 
schemes mentioned in Schedule—II of the above Act. 
(c) Government decided to bifurcate UTI to ring fence the liabilities 
on Government with regard to US-64 and assured return schemes of UTI; 
and to distance itself from the mutual fund activities of UTI which are 
regulated by SEBI. 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: Madam, the JPC has pointed out some 
serious charges on the part of the SEBI, RBI and the Ministry of Finance in 
connection with the erstwhile UTI's stock market dealings. May I know from 
the hon. Minister what steps are being taken to book the culprits, in 
accordance with the JPC Report? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: So far as taking action against the officials 
who have been found guilty of misdemeanour or misconduct, as the hon. 
Member knows, it is something that preceded the JPC's establishment. Action 
was taken against the officials; enquiry was ordered, and post enquiry, the 
matter has been referred to a Committee to look into what further action is to 
be taken against each of the officials. I can assure the hon. Member, without 
getting involved in the legalistic minutiae of what would be done or not, that 
those who have been found guilty of misconduct and are established as guilty 
of misconduct, will not be'spared; no one will be spared in that regard. 
 
6

[18 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: Madam, there was a report that the 
Government has given a massive amount of Rs. 14,500 crores in order to bail 
out the erstwhile UTI. What is the justification for putting such a burden on 
the exchequer, which was created by the scam? Would the hon. Minister 
explain it? The amount can be recovered from the culprits themselves. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, if I followed the question, what the 
hon. Member says is that he has, from somewhere, gathered the information 
that Rs. 14,000 plus crores have been paid by the Government, as he 
colourfully put it, to bail out the Unit Trust. I have shared every fact and 
information in this regard with the House when the Bill was enacted by the 
two Houses of Parliament. At that time, the figures were shared with the 
Members of the House. Let me again inform the hon. Member that so far as 
the money that has been paid, the funds given for Unit-64, is concerned, in 
2001 -02, it was Rs. 300 crores and for 2002-03, it was Rs. 938 crores, which 
makes a total of Rs. 1238 crores. On the assured return scheme, cash is nil, 
guarantees of Rs. 1000 crores and bonds worth Rs. 1118 crores. All this is for 
2002-03. A comfort letter has been provided to the Unit Trust to borrow from 
the banks and the comfort letter is of Rs. 450 crores. I have also some 
additional information. A Press release has also gone from the Department of 
Economic Affairs. No doubt, the hon. Member is aware of it. When I said that 
the Government shall honour the redemption scheme and we stand by our 
commitment to it, as this has been approved by the Cabinet. The liability on 
this account as currently calculated, because if we are required to fully 
redeem it, then it will be around Rs. 6000 crores. Now this is all the 
information that I can possibly share. It will be incorrect, therefore, to say that 
something like Rs. 14,000 crores has been paid out. That is an incorrect 
presumption. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: Madam Deputy Chairman, in the reply the 
reason for bifurcation of the UTI is stated to be 'to ring fence the liabilities on 
Government with regard to US-64 and assured return schemes of UTI.' What 
does it mean? Suppose, the UTI-I a nd the UTI-II finally again land in 
difficulty either due to mismanagement or due to some steps taken by the 
officials, then in that case, does the Government think that the Government 
will not be responsible for the amounts that have been deposited by the 
depositors? In the beginning when the UTI was set up, this was the assurance 
given that this is an organisation sponsored by 
 
7

RAJYA  SABHA [18 February, 2003] 
the Government of India. With that confidence in view, people have invested their 
money. What will be their fate if any such thing happens? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam Deputy Chairman, we have 
examined in great detail this very aspect and the Bill was enacted. I shared 
with the hon. Members then that the bifurcation is, in fact, to fencing the 
liability of the Government and the fencing in of Unit-I from Unit-ll. Let me 
very briefly explain the fundamental of it. Unit-I is Unit-64, the assured 
returned scheme and the special SUS, which was created with the public 
sector companies. The US-64 and the assured return scheme, the Government 
fully stands by. We have committed that we will honour it. In the month of June, 
the redemption will start. There is no question of the Government going back 
on that part of it. And the redemption scheme was announced long back. What 
we have done is to fence in Unit-64, the assured return scheme and SUS from 
Unit-ll. Unit-ll is a net asset value based mutual fund. This Mutual Fund, 
hereafter, governed by the SEBI Regulations is a Mutual Fund that will operate 
like any other Mutual Fund operates in the market. The question of 
mismanagement and, therefore, the Government withdrawing from it, etc., simply 
does not arise when it comes to UNIT-64. As far as UN IT-11 is concerned, it 
is a NAV-based Scheme. It is a Mutual Fund, SEBI regulated, market-controlled 
and this Scheme will, now, be governed, entirely, like any other Mutual Fund 
in the country.

SHRIJAGMOHAN: Madam, there are two parts of the question. One is 
the turndown. Everybody knows that after the September 11 incident, there 
was a downfall in the tourism all over the world. But after October, we have 
now changed the trend. In October, as compared to last October, there has 
been an increase of 16.8 per cent. Similarly, as compared to last November, 
there has been an increase of 16.2 per cent, and, then again, there has been 
another increase. In the month of January, as compared to the month of 
January of last year, the increase is about 22 per cent. So, in terms of number 
as well as in terms of earnings, there is now an upward trend. 
As regards the question why, during the last ten or fifteen years, the 
share of India in the world tourism ha s remained as low as .39 per cent, I 
think, the previous Governments had to answer that, but we are doing our best 
to now increase the tempo of tourism, and I am quite confident that with the 
new measures that we have taken, the setting up of all cultural-cum-tourism 
hubs and six tourism circuits all over the country—at least one in every big 
State is being done and the results are very obvious—there has been a 
tremendous increase in the domestic tourism. There was an increase of about 
24 per cent, in one year, in the domestic tourism. So, there has been an 
upward trend. The hon. Member has mentioned about China. Undoubtedly, 
China has made a tremendous increase. In this respect, we all have to 
understand why China has increased its tourism. One of the main reasons is 
that it is a highly disciplined society. But in our case, we must admit that all 
our tourist monuments are not kept clean; all types of slums, all types of 
stalls, all types of things come around, and whenever any action is taken, 
there is a problem. Everybody knows that. That is why, I think, under the new 
policy, we are emphasizing—and during the last one year, our measures have 
shown the results—that in almost all the areas we have taken special care of 
cleanliness. Ultimately, tourism is a civilisational issue; it all depends upon 
our value system, how we treat the people. How the taxJwallahs cheat the 
tourists, how the policemen cheat the people, how the customs men cheat the 
people, we are trying to look into all those aspects, and, I am sure, we will be 
able to show better results than the ones that have been there before.

Supply of gas from Iran 
*18. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether during his recent visit to India the Iranian President has 
made an offer of supply of gas to India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the proposed supply line for the transfer of 
gas will pass through Pakistan; 
(d) if so, what arrangements are proposed to be put in place to cover 
the security risk involved in a pipeline through Pakistan; 
(e) whether the proposed offer also includes a new global corporate 
ownership of the pipeline; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
RAM NAIK): (a) and (b) During the recent visit of President of Iran to India 
a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) has been signed between India and 
Iran for mutual cooperation in hydrocarbon sector including natural gas and 
LNG. As regards, import of natural gas from Iran, under bilateral 
cooperation, Indo-lran Joint Committee constituted a Joint Technical Sub-
Committee to assist it to explore all the options to import natural gas from 
Iran. The Joint Committee has decided to undertake an offshore feasibility 
study for laying of pipeline from Iran to India outside the Exclusive 
Economic Zone (EEZ) of Pakistan. Ga s Authority of Indi a Limited (GAIL) 
from India and National Iranian Gas Export Company (NIGEC) from Iran 
have been nominated as nodal agencies for the pipeline project by the 
respective Governments. Accordingly, GAIL and NIGEC have jointly 
commissioned an offshore pipeline feasibility study for the pipeline from Iran 
to India. Decision to take up the project would depend on technical feasibility 
and economic viability of the project. 
(c) to (f) No decision to import natural gas by on-land pipeline through 
Pakistan has been taken.

New exploration by ONGC 
*19. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the 
Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether after gas was found in Krishna Godavari Basin by 
Reliance, ONGC has also found gas in another exploration block at some 
other location; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when the exploration from the new source would start? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
RAM NAIK): (a) to (c) Subsequent to the announcement of the Krishna 
Godavari basin gas finds by the consortium of Reliance Industries Limited 
and Niko Resources Limited in October 2002. ONGC has found leads at 4 
new locations. Of these two leads, viz. Laiplmggaon in the upper Assam 
basin and Kavitam in the Krishna Godavari basin, are on land. The other two 
leads, viz. B-22-5 in Mumbai of shore and GS-KW in the Krishna Godavari 
basin, are offshore. 
ONGC had been awarded 24 exploration blocks by itself or in 
consortium with other Oil PSUs under the first and second round of New 
Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP). Of these 4 are on land. 11 are shallow 
off shore and 9 are deep water off shore blocks. Exploration activities have

Industries Limited and Niko Resources Limited, in October 2002, ONGC has 
been awarded 13 exploration blocks, i.e. 8 on-land. 3 shallow off-shore and 2

*20.  SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI: 
 SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have set up a Task Force on inter-linking of 
rivers; 
(b) if so, the details regarding composition of the task Force; 
(c) what are the terms of reference of the Task Force; 
(d) by when the Task Force is likely to submit its report; 
(e) whether the matter has been discussed with the State 
Governments; and 
(f) if so, by when the work on this project is likely to start? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN 
CHARAN SETHI): (a) to (d) A Task Force on Inter-linking of rivers under 
the Chairmanship of Shri Suresh P. Prabhu, Member of Parliament, Lok 
Sabha was constituted on 13.12.2002. Shri C.C. Patel and Dr. CD. Thatte, 
both Retd. Secretaries of the Ministry of Water Resources are Vice-Chairman 
and Member-Secretary of the Task Force respectively. Besides, the Task Force 
shall comprise of other Members (i) from water deficit States, (ii) from water 
surplus States, (iii) an economist, (iv) a sociologist and (v) a legal/world 
wildlife expert. 
The terms of reference of the Task Force are as under: 
(i) Provide guidance on norms of appraisal of individual projects in 
respect of economic viability, socio-economic impacts, 
environmental impacts and preparation of resettlement plans; 
(ii) devise suitable mechanism for bringing about speedy consensus 
amongst the States; 
(iii) Prioritize the different project components for preparation of 
Detailed Project Reports and implementation;

project; 
(v)    Consider various modalities for project funding; and 
(vi)   Consider international dimensions that may be involved in some 
project components. 
The Task Force is scheduled to prepare Action Plan I giving an outline 
of the time schedules for the completion of the feasibility studies, detailed 
project reports, estimated cost, implementation schedule, concrete benefits 
and advantages of the project, etc. by 30th April, 2003 and Action Plan li 
giving alternative options for funding and execution of the project as also the 
suggested methods for cost recovery by 31st July, 2003. 
(e) and (f) The Task Force is scheduled to deliberate over the project 
and to elicit the cooperation of the States by May/June 2003. The Chairman 
of the Task Force has visited and held informal consultation with several 
Chief Ministers of concerned States. As per the Milestones prepared by 
Government on inter-linking of rivers, feasibility studies on the Links and 
detailed project reports are Scheduled for completion by 31.12.2005 and 
31.12.2006 respectively. The project is scheduled for completion by the end 
of the year 2016.

Effect of Iraqi war on economy 
19. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any assessment of the likely 
effects of a possible war in Iraq on the Indian economy; and 
(b) if so, what are the main findings thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) 
and (b) The impact of possible war in Iraq on Indian economy will depend 
critically on the duration of conflict. Assuming a short and swift course, with 
a decisive US victory, the major impact would be on international crude oil 
prices, where in the country is well equipped to finance higher import bill in 
the event of a steep escalation of global oil prices or other exogenous 
developments. While there may be a temporary set back to our exports of 
goods and services to the gulf region, overall exports are unlikely to be 
affected too long. Remittances from the gulf region may also go down 
temporarily, the decline being preceded by a probable increase in remittances 
in anticipation of the conflict. With an observed tendency for a surplus in 
current account and comfortable foreign exchange reserves at more than $ 70 
billion, vulnerability of balance of payments to such changes, however, 
appears to be limited in the short run. 
Considering the current inflation rate and level of foodstocks, the 
impact on domestic inflation will be temporary, with hike in oil prices 
unlikely to result in any sharp surge in domestic inflation, Capital 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [18 February, 2003] 
markets may witness a slight stiffening of  interest rates, with limited decline 
in sentiments in stock markets followed by a quick recovery. Depending on 
market sentiments, the rupee may come under pressure, with such 
depreciation of the rupee, coupled with impact of oil price hike on domestic 
inflation, impinging on the current soft interest rate regime. 
Overall, the impact of possible war in Iraq on growth prospects of 
Indian economy is likely to be marginal in the short run. Notwithstanding 
such marginal impact on the economy, the overall growth performance of the 
Indian economy is unlikely to be seriously affected by the developments in 
the Gulf, due to clear signs of revival of domestic demand and the resultant 
buoyancy imparted to the domestic economy.

64. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of

126 

[18 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) The long-term 
observations made by the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) have shown 
a situation of fall in the level of ground water in various parts of the country.

(b) Water being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility 
of the concerned State Governments to plan, finance and execute 
schemes for augmenting water resources. The Central Government 
has initiated following measures to  recharge the underground water 
source:— 
(i)    Implementation of a Central Sector Scheme for Study of Recharge 
to Ground Water in the country. 
(ii) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground 
Water to the States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate 
area specific artificial recharge schemes to check the declining 
trend in ground water levels. 
(iii) Organisation of mass awareness programmes and training courses on 
rain water harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. 
(iv) Constitution of Central Ground Water Authority under the 
Environment (Protection) Act 1986  for regulation and control of 
ground water management and development. 
(c) Water being a State subject, suitable legislation for 
regulation and control of ground water development has to be 
enacted by the States/Union Territories. However, the Union 
Government has circulated a Model Bill to regulate and control the 
development of ground water in 1970, which was recirculated in 
1992 and again in 1996 to all the States/Union Territories for 
adoption.

Sale of minor girls in Orissa 
DR. M. N. DAS (Orissa) : My Special Mention might be relating to a 
particular State of our country, but the evil mentioned therein might be 
prevailing in other parts of India. Sir, while poverty of the tribal people of 
Orissa, particularly in Kalahandi, Bolangir and Koraput region - infamous as

the plight of the poorer people in coastal districts of Orissa, unscrupulous 
persons from outside are manipulating to smuggle out minor girls to other 
parts of India for making money from human misery. While a few instances of 
such deals come to light, majority of cases are never known. During 1994-
2001, according to Police sources, 3,286 minor-girls were reported missing 
from districts of Balasore, Bhadrak, ' Nayagarh, Cuttack and Mayurbhanj.

remaining hundreds remained untraced. Most of the victims belong to remote 
rural areas whose parents are too backward, besides being too poor, to try to 
recover their lost children. These children are perhaps sold for slavery purpose 
by inhuman locals to known agents from outside who are capable of deporting 
them to other States or even other countries.   It is also possible for merchants

ineffective before hunger and poverty, society has to intervene for effectively 
preventing abominable practices. Many measures can be thought of by the

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Mr. Vice-chairman, Sir, the

*25. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of communal clashes that took place during the last one 
year; 
(b) the number of persons killed and injured in these clashes; and 
(c) the details of steps taken by Government to enhance communal 
harmony? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) During last year (2002) 671 communal incidents have been 
reported to have taken place in the country in which 1126 persons were killed 
and 4138 persons sustained injuries. 
(c) A variety of measures are being taken in a sustained manner by the 
Central Government to assist the States in the maintenance of peace and 
communal harmony.These measures include sending alert messages and 
advisories, sharing of intelligence, providing Central Para-military Forces on 
specific request and assistance in the modernisation of Police forces. Detailed 
Guidelines to promote Communal Harmony have also been issued to all the 
States/Union Territories. 
Besides these administrative measures, the Union Government has also 
been taking promotional efforts like observance of the Annual Quami Ekta Week, 
conferment of Awards like Communal Harmony Awards and Kabir Puraskar and 
allotment of grants to Non-Governmental Organisations who are engaged in 
various programmes.for the promotion of communal harmony in the country.The 
National Foundation for Communal Harmony, an autonomous organisation 
under the Union Home Ministry is also engaged in various programmes for the 
promotion of Communal Harmony in the country.

Statement 
(a) to (c)The 15th Electric Power Survey estimated demand in the 
country. It was on the basis of 16th Electric Power Survey that the Working Group 
on Power for the 10th Plan constituted by the Planning Commission estimated the 
need based requirement of capacity addition of 55,158 MW for the 10th Plan. 
After discussions with the State Utilities and the Central Undertakings, it 
recommended a feasible capacity addition of 46,939 MW. The matter was further 
deliberated with the Planning Commission and depending upon the availability 
of resources and readiness of the projects a capacity addition target of 41,110 MW 
was settled. Effective mechanisms have been put in place to ensure timely 
completion of the projects and achievement of the targetted capacity during 
10th Plan.

supply position is expected to further improve through: 
An additional capacity of 3000 MW is expected to come from  
renewable sources of energy. In addition, supply of 1000 MW 
from Tala Hydroelectric Project in Bhutan is expected in the 
10th Plan. 
Undertaking energy conservation measures for which the 
Energy Conservation Act has been enacted and the Bureau of 
Energy Efficiency constituted. 
Reducing technical losses in distribution.The Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) is designed 
for the attainment of this objective. 
Undertaking Renovation Modernisation (R and M) of existing 
power stations which combined with improved Operation and 
Maintenance practices would lead to higher availability and 
generation. 
Export of power from surplus to deficit region through the gradual 
development of a National Grid to optimize utilization of 
generating capacity on an all India basis. 
Installation of capacity generating plants. The new Electricity 
Bill provides for a liberal framework for construction of 
captive power plants freely.

restructure the security arrangements in the country in the wake of attack on 
Indian Parliament on December 13,2001; 
(c) if so, the results thereof; 
(d) whether in Government's perception, there is a definite 
improvement in the security environment in the country and if so, the 
details thereof; and 
(e) what steps are being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) Major concerns of the current in ternal security

subversive activities of militant groups~(some of whom have trans-border bases)

and sharing of intelligence. The Central Government from time to time 
sensitises the State Governments with regard to internal security scenario 
prevailing in the country. The Central Government also provides assistance to the

there was complete breakdown of the Northern grid and Delhi and 
neighbouring States went without power;

regularity?

(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. There was neither 
any case of breakdown of the Northern Grid nor any incidence of Delhi and 
neighbouring States going without power during January, 2003. However, 
due to heavy fog and inclement weather during most part of January, 2003 the

hand, the flow of power from the Eastern part of Northern Region to the

line and also on account of restrictions imposed on some trunk transmission lines 
due to foggy weather conditions.

[19 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Shortages in the Northern Region especially in peak winter and 
summer months occur due to wide gap between requirement and availability of 
power. To bridge the gap between demand and availability, the short and 
medium term measures taken are as under:

Arrangements have been made enabling transfer of 500 MW of 
surplus power from Eastern Region to Northern Region through 
the recently commissioned HVDC back to back station,  
(ii) Early stabilization of newly commissioned units and overall 
increase in plant load factor of thermal units,  
(iii) Reduction in transmission and Distribution losses, 
 (iv) Renovation and Modernisation of old and inefficient thermal 
generating units,  
(v) Strengthening/Augmentation of sab-transmission and distribution 
systems of states under Accelerated Power Development and 
Reforms Programme,  
(vi) Demand side management and promotion of energy efficiency 
and conservation measures, 
 (vii) Exploitation of hydro potential at a faster pace.

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir, 
Hon'ble Prime Minister has launched a new initiative namely "Hariyali" on 
27.1.2003. Under this initiative, all watershed development programmes (DPAP, 
DDP and IWDP) of the Department of Land Resources would be implemented 
through Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRI).The basic features of "Hariyali" are 
given below: 
Under this initiative, the Gram Sabha would replace the Watershed 
Association and the Gram Panchayat would execute the watershed project with 
technical support from the Block Panchayat who would act as the Project 
Implementing Agency (PIA) for all watershed projects in a particular Block. In

Panchayats, suitable Government Line Department/Autonomous Agency may be 
identified for the purpose. Failing all these options, a reputed voluntary 
organization (NGO) of good operational/Financial standing in the district with 
adequate technical expertise and experience would be identified to act as the 
PIA.This initiative is applicable to all new watershed development projects to be 
sanctioned in future.

179. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the India cotton textiles industry, especially the spinning 
segments, is seeking improved market access before it concedes to pressures 
for lower import tariffs on textiles products; 
(b) if so, whether industry representatives were involved in the high level 
meetings of the groups formed to suggest steps relating to market access 
negotiations with respect to textile items; 
(c) whether the Union Government has accepted the suggestions of the 
industry representatives which seeks greater market access; and 
(d) if so, the steps and assistance being provided to the textile 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R.  PATIL): (a) to (c) Tariff negotiations on non-
agricultural products, including textiles, has commenced in the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO) following the Doha Ministerial Declaration. The 
objective of the negotiations is improvement in market access, in particular on 
products of export interest to developing countries. Further, developing countries 
are expected to offer less than full reciprocity in reduction commitments. 
The Textile Commissioner had constituted two Industry Groups for 
making recommendations on market access negotiations for textile items. The 
Industry Groups which included, representatives from Cotton Textile Industry, 
had made recommendations to the effect that reduction of import duties for textile 
products in India should be proposed provided there was more than comparable 
reduction in the import duties of our major importing countries, our competing 
countries effected similar reductions and Government took necessary decisions 
for improving the competitiveness of Indian textile industry. 
122 

[19 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA

WTO and once the modalities are finalised the actual tariff negotiations would begin. 
India has submitted its proposals on modalities to the WTO on 30th December, 
2002 after holding inter-ministerial discussions and consultations with other 
stakeholders. 
(d) Government have been taking several steps from time to time to 
strengthen the textile industry. Some of the important initiatives are:

operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector.

the rate of 50%. Cost of machinery has also been reduced through Fiscal

cotton for manufacture and export of competitive downstream textile 
products.

Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing.

exporters to get the textile products pre-tested for conforming to the 
requirements of importing countries.

SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, the Ninety-third

single scheme of the Department, the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, needs Rs.

least, 6 per cent of the GDP should be allocated for education. During the last 
decade, however, the State investment in education declined from an all-time 
high of almost 5 per cent of the GDP in 1991 to 3.6 per cent of the GDP in 
1997-98.

universalisation of elementary education in the next Budget; and, secondly, to 
ensure education of a reasonable quality for the children of socially and
